With no trainable parameters, CLUE only summarizes each reasoning trace by an hidden state delta and classifies correctness via nearest-centroid distance to ``success'' and ``failure'' clusters formed from past experience. The simplicity of this method highlights the strength of the underlying signal. Empirically, CLUE consistently outperforms LLM-as-a-judge baselines and matches or exceeds modern confidence-based methods in reranking candidates, improving both top-1 and majority-vote accuracy across AIME 24/25 and GPQA. As a highlight, on AIME 24 with a 1.5B model, CLUE boosts accuracy from 56.7% (majority@64) to 70.0% (top-maj@16).

papers.title: Inside-Out: Hidden Factual Knowledge in LLMs
papers.research_question: Does LLMs encode more factual knowledge in their parameters than they express in their outputs?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a formal framework to define and measure hidden factual knowledge in LLMs, demonstrating that LLMs encode more knowledge internally than they express externally.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents evidence of hidden knowledge in LLMs and calls for methods to surface internal knowledge more effectively for transparent and reliable models.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs consistently encode more factual knowledge internally than externally, with an average relative gap of 40%.
Some knowledge is so hidden that models can internally know an answer perfectly yet fail to generate it even after 1000 sampling attempts.
This reveals fundamental limitations in the generation capabilities of LLMs and constraints on scaling test-time compute.
papers.limitation: Results are a lower bound because only a single internal scoring function (probing) is used.
future_direction: Understanding reasons for differences in hidden knowledge across models
Developing methods to surface internal knowledge more effectively
papers.abstract: This work presents a framework for assessing whether large language models (LLMs) encode more factual knowledge in their parameters than what they express in their outputs. While a few studies hint at this possibility, none has clearly defined or demonstrated this phenomenon. We first propose a formal definition of knowledge, quantifying it for a given question as the fraction of correct-incorrect answer pairs where the correct one is ranked higher. This gives rise to external and internal knowledge, depending on the information used to score individual answer candidates: either the model's observable token-level probabilities or its intermediate computations. Hidden knowledge arises when internal knowledge exceeds external knowledge. We then present a case study, applying this framework to three popular open-weights LLMs in a closed-book QA setup. Our results indicate that: (1) LLMs consistently encode more factual knowledge internally than what they express externally, with an average relative gap of 40%. (2) Surprisingly, some knowledge is so deeply hidden that a model can internally know an answer perfectly, yet fail to generate it even once, despite large-scale repeated sampling of 1,000 answers. This reveals fundamental limitations in the generation capabilities of LLMs, which (3) put a practical constraint on scaling test-time compute via repeated answer sampling in closed-book QA: significant performance improvements remain inaccessible because some answers are practically never sampled, yet if they were, we would be guaranteed to rank them first.

papers.title: How Large Language Models Encode Context Knowledge? A Layer-Wise Probing Study
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode context knowledge across different layers?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a layer-wise probing framework to study how LLMs encode context knowledge, finding that more context knowledge is encoded in upper layers and that knowledge-related entity tokens encode knowledge earlier, with knowledge spreading to other tokens via attention.
papers.conclusion: Proposes a novel layer-wise probing framework for explaining how LLMs encode context knowledge, demonstrating that LLMs encode more knowledge in upper layers and transfer knowledge from entity tokens to other tokens, with retention diminishing with irrelevant evidence.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs prefer to encode more context knowledge in the upper layers.
LLMs primarily encode context knowledge within knowledge-related entity tokens at lower layers while progressively expanding more knowledge within other tokens at upper layers.
LLMs gradually forget the earlier context knowledge retained within the intermediate layers when provided with irrelevant evidence.
Base models have lower capability to encode knowledge through prompting compared to chat models.
The long-term memory capability of LLMs degrades when irrelevant evidence is introduced.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical mechanism behind the observed phenomena remains an open issue.
Experiments are limited to LLaMA 2 models, ignoring other SOTA models.
future_direction: Mathematical understanding of the role of self-attention in knowledge transfer.
Experiments on more PLMs (e.g., PaLM, OPT, Pythia).
papers.abstract: Previous work has showcased the intriguing capability of large language models (LLMs) in retrieving facts and processing context knowledge. However, only limited research exists on the layer-wise capability of LLMs to encode knowledge, which challenges our understanding of their internal mechanisms. In this paper, we devote the first attempt to investigate the layer-wise capability of LLMs through probing tasks. We leverage the powerful generative capability of ChatGPT to construct probing datasets, providing diverse and coherent evidence corresponding to various facts. We employ $\mathcal V$-usable information as the validation metric to better reflect the capability in encoding context knowledge across different layers. Our experiments on conflicting and newly acquired knowledge show that LLMs: (1) prefer to encode more context knowledge in the upper layers; (2) primarily encode context knowledge within knowledge-related entity tokens at lower layers while progressively expanding more knowledge within other tokens at upper layers; and (3) gradually forget the earlier context knowledge retained within the intermediate layers when provided with irrelevant evidence. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/Jometeorie/probing_llama.

papers.title: Decomposing Attention To Find Context-Sensitive Neurons
papers.research_question: How do transformer language models represent high-level contextual properties of text through attention mechanisms, and can we discover context-sensitive neurons from model weights using a calibration text?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to decompose attention in transformer language models, enabling the discovery of context-sensitive neurons from model weights using only a single calibration text, without requiring large-scale corpus activations.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that decomposing attention into positional and content components allows for the systematic discovery of context-sensitive neurons, advancing mechanistic interpretability by showing how first-layer heads create linear summaries of text context.
papers.key_findings:
First-layer attention heads with broad positional kernels and weak content dependence have stable softmax denominators across texts with fixed token distributions.
These stable heads can be approximated to construct linear summaries of the surrounding text, forming a contextual circuit.
Using this approximation, hundreds of first-layer neurons that respond to high-level contextual properties (e.g., Commonwealth vs American English) can be discovered from weights alone.
The contextual circuit approximation is highly correlated with true contributions, with a median correlation coefficient of 0.9485.
Neurons discovered this way do not require activation on the calibration text, reducing vulnerability to dataset artifacts.
papers.limitation: The approximation may underestimate contributions for texts with atypical token distributions, such as abnormal stop word density.
future_direction: Extend the decomposition to deeper layers of the model.
Explore how models with alternative positional schemes, like RoPE models, perform similar tasks.
Refine the approximation by clustering texts based on softmax denominator values.
papers.abstract: We study transformer language models, analyzing attention heads whose attention patterns are spread out, and whose attention scores depend weakly on content. We argue that the softmax denominators of these heads are stable when the underlying token distribution is fixed. By sampling softmax denominators from a "calibration text", we can combine together the outputs of multiple such stable heads in the first layer of GPT2-Small, approximating their combined output by a linear summary of the surrounding text. This approximation enables a procedure where from the weights alone - and a single calibration text - we can uncover hundreds of first layer neurons that respond to high-level contextual properties of the surrounding text, including neurons that didn't activate on the calibration text.

papers.title: Internal Consistency and Self-Feedback in Large Language Models: A Survey
papers.core_contribution: This survey provides a unified perspective on internal consistency in LLMs, introducing the Self-Feedback framework to categorize methods for improving reasoning and reducing hallucinations.
papers.conclusion: The survey concludes that internal consistency is a key challenge in LLMs and that Self-Feedback methods are promising for improving consistency, but more research is needed.
papers.key_findings:
Internal consistency can be viewed at three levels: response, decoding, and latent, and follows an hourglass evolution pattern.
Self-Feedback, consisting of Self-Evaluation and Self-Update, is an effective framework for mining internal consistency.
The survey categorizes existing methods into lines of work for reasoning elevation and hallucination alleviation.
The paper proposes the 'Consistency Is (Almost) Correctness' hypothesis and 'The Paradox of Latent and Explicit Reasoning'.
The survey addresses the question 'Does Self-Feedback Really Work?' with an in-depth analysis.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often exhibit deficient reasoning or generate hallucinations. To address these, studies prefixed with "Self-" such as Self-Consistency, Self-Improve, and Self-Refine have been initiated. They share a commonality: involving LLMs evaluating and updating themselves. Nonetheless, these efforts lack a unified perspective on summarization, as existing surveys predominantly focus on categorization. In this paper, we use a unified perspective of internal consistency, offering explanations for reasoning deficiencies and hallucinations. Internal consistency refers to the consistency in expressions among LLMs' latent, decoding, or response layers based on sampling methodologies. Then, we introduce an effective theoretical framework capable of mining internal consistency, named Self-Feedback. This framework consists of two modules: Self-Evaluation and Self-Update. The former captures internal consistency signals, while the latter leverages the signals to enhance either the model's response or the model itself. This framework has been employed in numerous studies. We systematically classify these studies by tasks and lines of work; summarize relevant evaluation methods and benchmarks; and delve into the concern, "Does Self-Feedback Really Work?" We also propose several critical viewpoints, including the "Hourglass Evolution of Internal Consistency", "Consistency Is (Almost) Correctness" hypothesis, and "The Paradox of Latent and Explicit Reasoning". The relevant resources are open-sourced at https://github.com/IAAR-Shanghai/ICSFSurvey.

papers.title: Calibrating Factual Knowledge in Pretrained Language Models
papers.research_question: How do we calibrate factual knowledge in Pretrained Language Models without re-training from scratch?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes CALINET, a lightweight method to calibrate factual knowledge in PLMs by adding and training new parameters (calibration memory slots) while freezing the original model, effectively reducing false knowledge and generalizing to downstream tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper reassesses knowledge in PLMs with CKA, proposes CALINET to calibrate knowledge at scale without updating original parameters, and shows it generalizes well to downstream tasks, with neuron-level investigations into the calibration mechanism.
papers.key_findings:
Contrastive Knowledge Assessment (CKA) reveals that nearly 50% of facts are stored incorrectly in PLMs.
CALINET effectively calibrates false facts, reducing the False Rate from 48.10% to 17.09% for T5-base on 100 facts.
CALINET generalizes calibrated knowledge to downstream question answering tasks, improving performance on calibration subsets without harming performance on other questions.
Analysis shows that calibration memory slots are more knowledge-intensive than original FFN values, with nearly 80% corresponding to meaningful concepts.
CALINET adjusts the output token distribution to increase the probability of the correct fact and its synonyms, indicating generalized calibration.
papers.limitation:
Relies on existing knowledge bases and synthetic data for assessment and calibration, which may not fully capture real-world knowledge complexity.
Evaluates PLMs via their predictions, which is a biased approach and may not accurately assess factual knowledge correctness.
Cannot completely calibrate all factual errors in PLMs.
future_direction: Improve calibration applicability in reality by moving beyond synthetic data.
Develop more accurate methods for assessing factual knowledge correctness in PLMs.
Develop more advanced knowledge calibration methods.
papers.abstract: Previous literature has proved that Pretrained Language Models (PLMs) can store factual knowledge. However, we find that facts stored in the PLMs are not always correct. It motivates us to explore a fundamental question: How do we calibrate factual knowledge in PLMs without re-training from scratch? In this work, we propose a simple and lightweight method CaliNet to achieve this goal. To be specific, we first detect whether PLMs can learn the right facts via a contrastive score between right and fake facts. If not, we then use a lightweight method to add and adapt new parameters to specific factual texts. Experiments on the knowledge probing task show the calibration effectiveness and efficiency. In addition, through closed-book question answering, we find that the calibrated PLM possesses knowledge generalization ability after finetuning.Beyond the calibration performance, we further investigate and visualize the knowledge calibration mechanism.

papers.title: Do LLMs Know about Hallucination? An Empirical Investigation of LLM's Hidden States
papers.research_question: Do LLMs possess awareness of hallucination, and if so, to what extent and through what mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Provides empirical evidence that LLMs exhibit awareness of hallucination through differences in hidden states when processing correct vs hallucinated answers, and shows potential for using hidden state guidance to mitigate hallucination.
papers.conclusion: LLMs possess awareness of hallucination as evidenced by differences in hidden states, and leveraging hidden state guidance can help mitigate hallucination.
papers.key_findings:
LLM’s final hidden state is more susceptible to be influenced by a correct answer compared to a hallucinated one.
Strategically inducing an LLM to produce hallucinated responses can raise its awareness consequently.
The level of awareness corresponds to the uncertainty of the LLM in the responses.
Providing relevant knowledge can assist LLMs in identifying hallucinated responses.
The transition between hidden states encodes truthfulness information.
papers.limitation:
Do not differentiate between fine-grained categories of hallucination.
Do not examine hidden states in intermediate transformer layers, only the final layer.
Experiments are performed on conventional QA tasks, not more complicated or domain-specific tasks.
Future research is needed to develop more effective strategies for mitigating LLM hallucination.
future_direction: Explore different types of hallucination (factual fabrication, instruction inconsistency, etc.).
Examine hidden states in intermediate transformer layers and investigate layer-by-layer formation of hallucination.
Adapt the experimental framework to more complicated or domain-specific tasks and potentially extend to multimodal features.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can make up answers that are not real, and this is known as hallucination. This research aims to see if, how, and to what extent LLMs are aware of hallucination. More specifically, we check whether and how an LLM reacts differently in its hidden states when it answers a question right versus when it hallucinates. To do this, we introduce an experimental framework which allows examining LLM's hidden states in different hallucination situations. Building upon this framework, we conduct a series of experiments with language models in the LLaMA family (Touvron et al., 2023). Our empirical findings suggest that LLMs react differently when processing a genuine response versus a fabricated one. We then apply various model interpretation techniques to help understand and explain the findings better. Moreover, informed by the empirical observations, we show great potential of using the guidance derived from LLM's hidden representation space to mitigate hallucination. We believe this work provides insights into how LLMs produce hallucinated answers and how to make them occur less often.

papers.title: Do Retrieval Augmented Language Models Know When They Don't Know?
papers.research_question: Do retrieval-augmented language models (RALMs) know when they don't know? Specifically, the paper investigates three questions: 1) Are RALMs well calibrated with respect to different internal and external knowledge states? 2) How does a RALM's refusal ability align with its calibration quality? 3) Can we combine refusal-aware RALMs with uncertainty-based answer abstention to mitigate over-refusal?
papers.core_contribution: The paper investigates the calibration and refusal behavior of RALMs, identifies an over-refusal problem when models are confronted with irrelevant contexts, and proposes a two-stage refusal technique to improve overall answer quality by balancing refusal and correct answers.
papers.conclusion: The study offers insights that underscore the need for improved calibration methods and the explicit modeling of dynamically evolving knowledge in RALMs.
papers.key_findings:
RALMs exhibit significant over-refusal behavior when confronted with exclusively irrelevant contexts, refusing questions they could have answered correctly.
The over-refusal problem can be mitigated by in-context fine-tuning (ICFT) but is exacerbated by R-tuning.
Improved refusal behavior does not necessarily imply better calibration or higher overall accuracy, due to changes in robustness and contextual faithfulness.
A two-stage refusal technique that first infers the model's knowledge state and then applies a refusal threshold can mitigate over-refusal and improve overall response quality.
future_direction: Uncertainty estimation for RALMs remains an open problem deserving deeper investigation.
papers.abstract: Existing large language models (LLMs) occasionally generate plausible yet factually incorrect responses, known as hallucinations. Two main approaches have been proposed to mitigate hallucinations: retrieval-augmented language models (RALMs) and refusal post-training. However, current research predominantly focuses on their individual effectiveness while overlooking the evaluation of the refusal capability of RALMs. Ideally, if RALMs know when they do not know, they should refuse to answer.In this study, we ask the fundamental question: Do RALMs know when they don't know? Specifically, we investigate three questions. First, are RALMs well calibrated with respect to different internal and external knowledge states? We examine the influence of various factors. Contrary to expectations, when all retrieved documents are irrelevant, RALMs still tend to refuse questions they could have answered correctly. Next, given the model's pronounced \textbf{over-refusal} behavior, we raise a second question: How does a RALM's refusal ability align with its calibration quality? Our results show that the over-refusal problem can be mitigated through in-context fine-tuning. However, we observe that improved refusal behavior does not necessarily imply better calibration or higher overall accuracy. Finally, we ask: Can we combine refusal-aware RALMs with uncertainty-based answer abstention to mitigate over-refusal? We develop a simple yet effective refusal mechanism for refusal-post-trained RALMs that improves their overall answer quality by balancing refusal and correct answers. Our study provides a more comprehensive understanding of the factors influencing RALM behavior. Meanwhile, we emphasize that uncertainty estimation for RALMs remains an open problem deserving deeper investigation.

papers.title: Inspecting and Editing Knowledge Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we map natural language statements to fact encodings in an LM's internal representations to enable editing and probing of knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: REMEDI is a method that learns to map natural language statements to fact encodings in LM representations, enabling both editing of knowledge (by adding vectors to hidden representations) and probing of existing knowledge.
papers.conclusion: REMEDI links work on probing, prompting, and LM editing, and offers steps toward general tools for fine-grained inspection and control of knowledge in LMs.
papers.key_findings:
REMEDI can patch errors made by an LM and insert new facts with or without context provided in the prompt.
REMEDI can help detect errors before generation by comparing edit vectors to unedited representations.
REMEDI increases accuracy on occupation classification and factual editing tasks compared to prompting baselines.
REMEDI generalizes from out-of-context training to in-context editing, suggesting unified representation of background and contextual knowledge.
REMEDI edits preserve correlations between features (e.g., adding 'made of metal' increases probability of 'shiny').
papers.limitation:
REMEDI can occasionally lead to disfluent or incorrect generations.
REMEDI sometimes damages the essence of the entity (e.g., making Wiener schnitzel an anime instead of a food).
REMEDI can also cause unrelated facts to change (e.g., changing the air dates of a TV show).
future_direction: Developing controlled generation interfaces that allow direct steering of model behavior in representation space.
Building tools for monitoring and controlling language generation by directly specifying facts and situations in an LM's native encoding scheme.
papers.abstract: Neural language models (LMs) represent facts about the world described by text. Sometimes these facts derive from training data (in most LMs, a representation of the word "banana" encodes the fact that bananas are fruits). Sometimes facts derive from input text itself (a representation of the sentence "I poured out the bottle" encodes the fact that the bottle became empty). We describe REMEDI, a method for learning to map statements in natural language to fact encodings in an LM's internal representation system. REMEDI encodings can be used as knowledge editors: when added to LM hidden representations, they modify downstream generation to be consistent with new facts. REMEDI encodings may also be used as probes: when compared to LM representations, they reveal which properties LMs already attribute to mentioned entities, in some cases making it possible to predict when LMs will generate outputs that conflict with background knowledge or input text. REMEDI thus links work on probing, prompting, and LM editing, and offers steps toward general tools for fine-grained inspection and control of knowledge in LMs.

papers.title: Overthinking the Truth: Understanding how Language Models Process False Demonstrations
papers.research_question: Why do language models imitate incorrect demonstrations in their context, and how does this behavior emerge internally?
papers.core_contribution: Language models 'overthink' when given false few-shot demonstrations, and this harmful imitation is caused by specific 'false induction heads' in late layers that attend to and copy incorrect labels from the context.
papers.conclusion: Studying intermediate model computations, such as through the logit lens and head ablation, is a promising avenue for understanding and mitigating harmful context-following behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
Given incorrect demonstrations, model accuracy decreases in later layers after a 'critical layer', a phenomenon termed 'overthinking'.
Ablating late layers or specific attention heads improves accuracy on incorrect demonstrations, indicating these components are responsible for the harmful imitation.
False induction heads are identified as attention heads in late layers that attend to and promote false labels from previous demonstrations.
Ablating a small set of false induction heads reduces the accuracy gap between correct and incorrect prompts by an average of 38.9% across 14 datasets.
The overthinking phenomenon and the role of false induction heads are consistent across multiple model families and sizes.
future_direction: Building tools to understand intermediate computations to proactively understand and reduce harmful model behaviors.
Applying insights to detect and guard against prompt injection attacks.
papers.abstract: Modern language models can imitate complex patterns through few-shot learning, enabling them to complete challenging tasks without fine-tuning. However, imitation can also lead models to reproduce inaccuracies or harmful content if present in the context. We study harmful imitation through the lens of a model's internal representations, and identify two related phenomena: "overthinking" and "false induction heads". The first phenomenon, overthinking, appears when we decode predictions from intermediate layers, given correct vs. incorrect few-shot demonstrations. At early layers, both demonstrations induce similar model behavior, but the behavior diverges sharply at some "critical layer", after which the accuracy given incorrect demonstrations progressively decreases. The second phenomenon, false induction heads, are a possible mechanistic cause of overthinking: these are heads in late layers that attend to and copy false information from previous demonstrations, and whose ablation reduces overthinking. Beyond scientific understanding, our results suggest that studying intermediate model computations could be a promising avenue for understanding and guarding against harmful model behaviors.

papers.title: Do I Know This Entity? Knowledge Awareness and Hallucinations in Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the mechanisms behind hallucinations in language models, specifically regarding entity recognition and knowledge awareness?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers entity recognition directions in the representation space that encode knowledge awareness and shows they causally affect knowledge refusal and hallucinations.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that language models have internal representations of knowledge awareness that affect refusal and hallucinations, and that chat fine-tuning repurposes this existing mechanism.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders uncover directions in the representation space that detect whether the model recognizes an entity as known or unknown.
These entity recognition directions generalize across diverse entity types (players, movies, cities, songs).
The directions causally affect knowledge refusal: steering can induce the model to refuse on known entities or hallucinate on unknown entities.
The directions disrupt the attention of downstream heads in the factual recall circuit, suppressing attribute extraction.
Early entity recognition directions regulate the model's expression of knowledge uncertainty, and uncertainty directions are predictive of incorrect answers.
papers.limitation: The methodology for labeling entities as known or unknown might introduce inaccuracies, as the model could guess attributes or fail to recall specific attributes while knowing about the entity.
papers.abstract: Hallucinations in large language models are a widespread problem, yet the mechanisms behind whether models will hallucinate are poorly understood, limiting our ability to solve this problem. Using sparse autoencoders as an interpretability tool, we discover that a key part of these mechanisms is entity recognition, where the model detects if an entity is one it can recall facts about. Sparse autoencoders uncover meaningful directions in the representation space, these detect whether the model recognizes an entity, e.g. detecting it doesn't know about an athlete or a movie. This suggests that models can have self-knowledge: internal representations about their own capabilities. These directions are causally relevant: capable of steering the model to refuse to answer questions about known entities, or to hallucinate attributes of unknown entities when it would otherwise refuse. We demonstrate that despite the sparse autoencoders being trained on the base model, these directions have a causal effect on the chat model's refusal behavior, suggesting that chat finetuning has repurposed this existing mechanism. Furthermore, we provide an initial exploration into the mechanistic role of these directions in the model, finding that they disrupt the attention of downstream heads that typically move entity attributes to the final token.

papers.title: Probing Latent Knowledge Conflict for Faithful Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.research_question: How can we improve contextual faithfulness in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems by moving beyond black-box interventions and analyzing the model's internal reasoning process? Specifically, how is conflict represented in the model's latent space and how does it disrupt faithful generation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces ProbeRAG, a framework that leverages latent probing to detect knowledge conflicts in the model's hidden states and uses conflict-aware attention modulation to improve contextual faithfulness in RAG systems.
papers.conclusion: ProbeRAG effectively improves contextual faithfulness in RAG by moving beyond black-box interventions to internal guidance, demonstrating consistent and robust performance across various models and datasets.
papers.key_findings:
Conflicting and aligned knowledge states are linearly separable in the model's latent space, providing a detectable 'conflict feature'.
Contextual noise systematically increases the entropy of these representations, obscuring the conflict feature.
ProbeRAG, which integrates fine-grained knowledge pruning, latent conflict probing, and conflict-aware attention, substantially improves accuracy and contextual faithfulness across multiple benchmarks and models.
The accuracy of the conflict probe is positively correlated with the model's ability to generate faithful responses.
Attention visualization shows that after training with the attention-guidance loss, the model allocates more attention to tokens marked as conflicting knowledge.
papers.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has emerged as a powerful paradigm to enhance the factuality of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, existing RAG systems often suffer from an unfaithfulness issue, where the model's response contradicts evidence from the retrieved context. Existing approaches to improving contextual faithfulness largely rely on external interventions, such as prompt engineering, decoding constraints, or reward-based fine-tuning. These works treat the LLM as a black box and overlook a crucial question: how does the LLM internally integrate retrieved evidence with its parametric memory, particularly under knowledge conflicts? To address this gap, we conduct a probing-based analysis of hidden-state representations in LLMs and observe three findings: knowledge integration occurs hierarchically, conflicts manifest as latent signals at the sentence level, and irrelevant context is often amplified when aligned with parametric knowledge. Building on these findings, we propose CLEAR (Conflict-Localized and Enhanced Attention for RAG), a framework that (i) decomposes context into fine-grained sentence-level knowledge, (ii) employs hidden-state probing to localize conflicting knowledge, and (iii) introduces conflict-aware fine-tuning to guide the model to accurately integrate retrieved evidence. Extensive experiments across three benchmarks demonstrate that CLEAR substantially improves both accuracy and contextual faithfulness, consistently outperforming strong baselines under diverse conflict conditions. The related resources are available at https://github.com/LinfengGao/CLEAR.

papers.title: Truth-value judgment in language models:belief directions are context sensitive
papers.research_question: How does context impact the behavior of belief probes (directions predictive of truth) in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates the context sensitivity and consistency of belief probes across layers and models, shows belief directions are causal mediators in natural language inference, and introduces a more stable variant of Contrast Consistent Search (CCR).
papers.conclusion: The results suggest that belief directions are causal mediators in the inference process that incorporates in-context information.
papers.key_findings:
Belief probes are generally context sensitive but are also sensitive to irrelevant contexts and can update probabilities incorrectly.
The type of errors made by probes depend on the layer, the model type, and the kind of data.
Belief directions are (one of the) causal mediators in the inference process that incorporates in-context information.
Instruction-tuning makes models more likely to represent prior assertions as true, even if they conflict with the model's own evaluation.
papers.limitation: The difficulty of separating hypothetical LLM 'beliefs' from commonly-held beliefs, as probes might identify features correlated with truth in the training data rather than an objective evaluation of truth.
papers.abstract: Recent work has demonstrated that the latent spaces of large language models (LLMs) contain directions predictive of the truth of sentences. Multiple methods recover such directions and build probes that are described as getting at a model's "knowledge" or "beliefs". We investigate this phenomenon, looking closely at the impact of context on the probes. Our experiments establish where in the LLM the probe's predictions can be described as being conditional on the preceding (related) sentences. Specifically, we quantify the responsiveness of the probes to the presence of (negated) supporting and contradicting sentences, and score the probes on their consistency. We also perform a causal intervention experiment, investigating whether moving the representation of a premise along these belief directions influences the position of the hypothesis along that same direction. We find that the probes we test are generally context sensitive, but that contexts which should not affect the truth often still impact the probe outputs. Our experiments show that the type of errors depend on the layer, the (type of) model, and the kind of data. Finally, our results suggest that belief directions are (one of the) causal mediators in the inference process that incorporates in-context information.

papers.title: Emergence of Linear Truth Encodings in Language Models
papers.research_question: Why and how do linear truth subspaces that separate true from false statements emerge in language models during training and inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that linear truth encodings in language models can emerge from the statistical co-occurrence of true/false statements (Truth Co-occurrence Hypothesis), demonstrated through a toy transformer model and experiments.
papers.conclusion: Linear truth encodings in language models can emerge from the co-occurrence statistics of true and false statements, as demonstrated by a toy model and supported by experiments in pretrained models.
papers.key_findings:
Linear truth encoding emerges in a one-layer transformer trained on data where true/false statements co-occur (Truth Co-occurrence Hypothesis).
Training exhibits two phases: fast memorization of factual associations followed by slower development of linear truth separation.
Layer normalization is necessary for the linear separability of true and false representations.
The value matrix develops a block structure that enables sharpening of predictions for true sequences.
Experiments with Pythia-6.9B show similar two-phase dynamics in a large pretrained model.
papers.limitation:
The toy model is far simpler than natural training data, so the mechanism might not fully capture real-world complexity.
In real LMs, additional mechanisms likely contribute to truth encoding.
future_direction: Systematic study of mechanisms for truth encoding in real LMs.
Generalization of truth encoding across different relations.
papers.abstract: Recent probing studies reveal that large language models exhibit linear subspaces that separate true from false statements, yet the mechanism behind their emergence is unclear. We introduce a transparent, one-layer transformer toy model that reproduces such truth subspaces end-to-end and exposes one concrete route by which they can arise. We study one simple setting in which truth encoding can emerge: a data distribution where factual statements co-occur with other factual statements (and vice-versa), encouraging the model to learn this distinction in order to lower the LM loss on future tokens. We corroborate this pattern with experiments in pretrained language models. Finally, in the toy setting we observe a two-phase learning dynamic: networks first memorize individual factual associations in a few steps, then -- over a longer horizon -- learn to linearly separate true from false, which in turn lowers language-modeling loss. Together, these results provide both a mechanistic demonstration and an empirical motivation for how and why linear truth representations can emerge in language models.

papers.title: Analysing the Residual Stream of Language Models Under Knowledge Conflicts
papers.research_question: Can we identify the conflict between context and parameter knowledge by probing the residual stream? Can we know which source of knowledge the models will use before they generate the answers?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs internally register knowledge conflict signals in the residual stream, which can be detected by probing intermediate activations. The residual stream shows distinct skewness patterns when the model relies on contextual versus parametric knowledge, enabling prediction of the model's knowledge selection behavior.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit internal mechanisms for identifying conflicts in the mid-layers, and the residual stream shows distinct skewness patterns when the model uses context and parametric knowledge to predict. This analysis provides insights into the behaviour of LLMs in the presence of knowledge conflicts.
papers.key_findings:
The signal of knowledge conflict rises from intermediate layers (e.g., layer 13-14) and can be detected with high accuracy using linear probing.
The residual stream exhibits different skewness patterns (measured by Kurtosis, Hoyer, Gini) when the model uses contextual knowledge versus parametric knowledge.
The decision of which knowledge to use occurs after the detection of the knowledge conflict signal.
The probing model's performance for conflict detection peaks around the 14th layer and then decreases slightly.
The skewness patterns are more pronounced in hidden states than in MLP or Self-Attention activations.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can store a significant amount of factual knowledge in their parameters. However, their parametric knowledge may conflict with the information provided in the context. Such conflicts can lead to undesirable model behaviour, such as reliance on outdated or incorrect information. In this work, we investigate whether LLMs can identify knowledge conflicts and whether it is possible to know which source of knowledge the model will rely on by analysing the residual stream of the LLM. Through probing tasks, we find that LLMs can internally register the signal of knowledge conflict in the residual stream, which can be accurately detected by probing the intermediate model activations. This allows us to detect conflicts within the residual stream before generating the answers without modifying the input or model parameters. Moreover, we find that the residual stream shows significantly different patterns when the model relies on contextual knowledge versus parametric knowledge to resolve conflicts. This pattern can be employed to estimate the behaviour of LLMs when conflict happens and prevent unexpected answers before producing the answers. Our analysis offers insights into how LLMs internally manage knowledge conflicts and provides a foundation for developing methods to control the knowledge selection processes.

papers.title: Know More, Know Clearer: A Meta-Cognitive Framework for Knowledge Augmentation in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we bridge the knowledge-confidence gaps in Large Language Models (LLMs) during knowledge augmentation to enhance knowledge capabilities and foster cognitive behaviors that better distinguish knowns from unknowns?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a meta-cognitive framework that uses internal cognitive signals to partition the knowledge space into mastered, confused, and missing regions for targeted knowledge expansion, and introduces a cognitive consistency mechanism to align subjective certainty with objective accuracy, thereby enhancing knowledge capabilities and clarifying knowledge boundaries.
papers.conclusion: Knowledge augmentation is not merely a matter of acquiring more knowledge, but of knowing more clearly what they know and what they do not.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed framework (CGKE + CDKC) significantly outperforms strong baselines across diverse QA benchmarks.
Iterative evolution with two full 'expansion-calibration' cycles yields substantial additional performance gains.
The framework improves the correlation between internal confidence and accuracy, indicating enhanced meta-cognitive alignment.
Ablation studies show that resolving cognitive ambiguity (Knowledge Confused region) is more impactful for expanding knowledge boundaries than reinforcing mastered facts.
The framework demonstrates robustness across varying knowledge grounding states (weakly, partially, and well-grounded).
papers.abstract: Knowledge augmentation has significantly enhanced the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) in knowledge-intensive tasks. However, existing methods typically operate on the simplistic premise that model performance equates with internal knowledge, overlooking the knowledge-confidence gaps that lead to overconfident errors or uncertain truths. To bridge this gap, we propose a novel meta-cognitive framework for reliable knowledge augmentation via differentiated intervention and alignment. Our approach leverages internal cognitive signals to partition the knowledge space into mastered, confused, and missing regions, guiding targeted knowledge expansion. Furthermore, we introduce a cognitive consistency mechanism to synchronize subjective certainty with objective accuracy, ensuring calibrated knowledge boundaries. Extensive experiments demonstrate the our framework consistently outperforms strong baselines, validating its rationality in not only enhancing knowledge capabilities but also fostering cognitive behaviors that better distinguish knowns from unknowns.

papers.title: Mind Scramble: Unveiling Large Language Model Psychology Via Typoglycemia
papers.research_question: Does LLM possess human-like cognitive processes and mechanisms in reading and comprehending? The paper uses Typoglycemia to explore this.
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces LLM Psychology, a framework that uses Typoglycemia experiments to study cognitive behaviors of LLMs. It finds that LLMs exhibit human-like behaviors but are fundamentally data-driven, and each LLM has a unique cognitive pattern.
papers.conclusion: The study advances research on aligning LLMs with human cognition and provides evidence that LLMs' abilities are data-driven, offering a case for LLM Psychology.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs demonstrate human-like behaviors on a macro scale, such as slightly lower task accuracy with consuming more tokens and time.
Different LLMs show varying degrees of robustness to scrambled input, making it a democratized benchmark for model evaluation.
The impact of different task types varies, with complex logical tasks (e.g., math) in scrambled format being more challenging.
LLMs' emergent human-like abilities are fundamentally statistical and data-driven, rather than genuinely resembling human cognition.
Each LLM exhibits its unique and consistent 'cognitive pattern' across various tasks, unveiling a general mechanism in its psychology process.
papers.abstract: Research into the external behaviors and internal mechanisms of large language models (LLMs) has shown promise in addressing complex tasks in the physical world. Studies suggest that powerful LLMs, like GPT-4, are beginning to exhibit human-like cognitive abilities, including planning, reasoning, and reflection. In this paper, we introduce a research line and methodology called LLM Psychology, leveraging human psychology experiments to investigate the cognitive behaviors and mechanisms of LLMs. We migrate the Typoglycemia phenomenon from psychology to explore the "mind" of LLMs. Unlike human brains, which rely on context and word patterns to comprehend scrambled text, LLMs use distinct encoding and decoding processes. Through Typoglycemia experiments at the character, word, and sentence levels, we observe: (I) LLMs demonstrate human-like behaviors on a macro scale, such as lower task accuracy and higher token/time consumption; (II) LLMs exhibit varying robustness to scrambled input, making Typoglycemia a benchmark for model evaluation without new datasets; (III) Different task types have varying impacts, with complex logical tasks (e.g., math) being more challenging in scrambled form; (IV) Each LLM has a unique and consistent "cognitive pattern" across tasks, revealing general mechanisms in its psychology process. We provide an in-depth analysis of hidden layers to explain these phenomena, paving the way for future research in LLM Psychology and deeper interpretability.

papers.title: Direct Confidence Alignment: Aligning Verbalized Confidence with Internal Confidence In Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we align a Large Language Model's verbalized confidence (expressed in words) with its internal confidence (derived from token probabilities) to improve model transparency and reliability?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Direct Confidence Alignment (DCA), a method using Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) to align an LLM's verbalized confidence with its internal confidence, improving transparency. Results show DCA is effective on some model architectures (e.g., Gemma-2-9B-Instruct) but ineffective on others, highlighting the need for model-aware approaches.
papers.conclusion: DCA can improve alignment between verbalized and internal confidence in some LLMs, but its effectiveness varies across architectures, underscoring the need for further improvements and model-aware alignment strategies.
papers.key_findings:
DCA improved confidence alignment metrics (e.g., Spearman's ρ, mean absolute calibration error) consistently for Gemma-2-9B-Instruct across all datasets.
DCA produced mixed results for Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct and Mistral-7B-Instruct, sometimes degrading alignment and accuracy, indicating the method's effectiveness is model-dependent.
DCA reduced the variance in calibration error (σ_ϵ and σ_M) for most models, suggesting it makes confidence expression more consistent.
DCA had mixed impacts on model accuracy: it increased accuracy for Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, decreased it for Mistral-7B-Instruct, and left Gemma-2-9B-Instruct's accuracy largely unchanged.
The effectiveness of DCA appears to be more dependent on model architecture than on the specific task or dataset.
papers.limitation:
The method requires access to internal logits to extract internal confidence, making it inapplicable to closed-source models.
The method relies on the assumption that the model's internal confidence (from token probabilities) is better calibrated than its verbalized confidence, which may not always hold.
DCA can degrade model accuracy because the preference dataset includes incorrect answers, and the method does not directly optimize for correctness.
future_direction: Expanding the method to be compatible with a wider range of model architectures.
Exploring more strategies to improve the alignment between verbalized and internal confidence.
Developing strategies to mitigate the potential degradation of model accuracy caused by DCA.
papers.abstract: Producing trustworthy and reliable Large Language Models (LLMs) has become increasingly important as their usage becomes more widespread. Calibration seeks to achieve this by improving the alignment between the model's confidence and the actual likelihood of its responses being correct or desirable. However, it has been observed that the internal confidence of a model, derived from token probabilities, is not well aligned with its verbalized confidence, leading to misleading results with different calibration methods. In this paper, we propose Direct Confidence Alignment (DCA), a method using Direct Preference Optimization to align an LLM's verbalized confidence with its internal confidence rather than ground-truth accuracy, enhancing model transparency and reliability by ensuring closer alignment between the two confidence measures. We evaluate DCA across multiple open-weight LLMs on a wide range of datasets. To further assess this alignment, we also introduce three new calibration error-based metrics. Our results show that DCA improves alignment metrics on certain model architectures, reducing inconsistencies in a model's confidence expression. However, we also show that it can be ineffective on others, highlighting the need for more model-aware approaches in the pursuit of more interpretable and trustworthy LLMs.

papers.title: Transformers represent belief state geometry in their residual stream
papers.research_question: What computational structure are we building into large language models when we train them on next-token prediction? Specifically, is the structure given by the meta-dynamics of belief updating over hidden states of the data-generating process, and are belief states linearly represented in the residual stream?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a theoretical framework and empirical evidence that transformers trained on next-token prediction linearly represent the geometry of belief states (from the mixed-state presentation of the data-generating process) in their residual stream, even for complex fractal geometries, and that this representation captures information beyond local next-token predictions.
papers.conclusion: Transformers construct predictive representations that encode the complex geometry of belief updating over hidden states, capturing an inference process over the underlying structure of the data-generating process, which provides a concrete link between training data structure and internal model representations.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers trained on data from hidden Markov models (HMMs) linearly represent the belief state geometry of the mixed-state presentation in their residual stream, as verified by linear regression.
The belief state representation emerges during training and is not an artifact, as shown by controls including cross-validation and shuffling.
For processes where distinct belief states share the same next-token distribution (e.g., RRXOR), the belief state geometry is not well represented in the final layer alone but is distributed across multiple layers of the residual stream.
The representation captures information about the entire future distribution, not just the next token, as demonstrated by comparing pairwise distances between belief states versus next-token probabilities.
The belief state geometry is robust to the choice of using pre- or post-layer normalization activations.
papers.limitation:
Experimental validation focused on small-scale systems (HMMs with 3-5 states and vocabularies of 2-3 tokens), a significant simplification compared to modern language models.
For realistic systems, the dimensionality of the belief state simplex would exceed the residual stream dimension, suggesting representation must be compressed; the nature of this compression is not understood.
Explicitly computing ground-truth belief states becomes intractable as the size of the minimal generating structure and context window length grows, requiring new methodologies for validation in larger settings.
The work is limited to the stationary ergodic setting, though the framework is expected to extend to non-stationary and non-ergodic processes.
The paper establishes the representation of belief states but does not test whether transformers implement a circuit for performing Bayesian updates.
future_direction: Extending the framework to non-stationary and non-ergodic processes, such as in-context learning.
Understanding how belief state geometry is compressed when the simplex dimension exceeds the residual stream dimension.
Investigating the mapping between belief states and features, which is likely complex and architecture-dependent.
papers.abstract: What computational structure are we building into large language models when we train them on next-token prediction? Here, we present evidence that this structure is given by the meta-dynamics of belief updating over hidden states of the data-generating process. Leveraging the theory of optimal prediction, we anticipate and then find that belief states are linearly represented in the residual stream of transformers, even in cases where the predicted belief state geometry has highly nontrivial fractal structure. We investigate cases where the belief state geometry is represented in the final residual stream or distributed across the residual streams of multiple layers, providing a framework to explain these observations. Furthermore we demonstrate that the inferred belief states contain information about the entire future, beyond the local next-token prediction that the transformers are explicitly trained on. Our work provides a general framework connecting the structure of training data to the geometric structure of activations inside transformers.

papers.title: LLM Assertiveness can be Mechanistically Decomposed into Emotional and Logical Components
papers.research_question: What is the internal basis of LLM assertiveness, and can it be decomposed into separable components like emotional and logical persuasion?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that LLM assertiveness can be mechanistically decomposed into orthogonal emotional and logical components, providing evidence for a multi-component structure similar to human persuasion models.
papers.conclusion: The study provides mechanistic evidence for the multi-component structure of LLM assertiveness and highlights avenues for mitigating overconfident behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Middle layers (5-6) are most sensitive to assertiveness contrasts.
High-assertive representations decompose into orthogonal emotional and logical clusters.
Emotional steering vectors broadly influence prediction accuracy, whereas logical vectors have more localized effects.
papers.limitation:
The model is small (1B parameters), so scaling effects are uncertain.
Only one architecture is examined, limiting cross-model generality.
Dataset size is modest (n=645), which may obscure finer-grained cues.
Cluster interpretation relies on manual inspection.
future_direction: Develop more automated approaches for cluster interpretation.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often display overconfidence, presenting information with unwarranted certainty in high-stakes contexts. We investigate the internal basis of this behavior via mechanistic interpretability. Using open-sourced Llama 3.2 models fine-tuned on human annotated assertiveness datasets, we extract residual activations across all layers, and compute similarity metrics to localize assertive representations. Our analysis identifies layers most sensitive to assertiveness contrasts and reveals that high-assertive representations decompose into two orthogonal sub-components of emotional and logical clusters-paralleling the dual-route Elaboration Likelihood Model in Psychology. Steering vectors derived from these sub-components show distinct causal effects: emotional vectors broadly influence prediction accuracy, while logical vectors exert more localized effects. These findings provide mechanistic evidence for the multi-component structure of LLM assertiveness and highlight avenues for mitigating overconfident behavior.

papers.title: Vision-Language Introspection: Mitigating Overconfident Hallucinations in MLLMs via Interpretable Bi-Causal Steering
papers.research_question: How to mitigate overconfident hallucinations in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) by simulating a metacognitive self-correction process that diagnoses and rectifies internal visual-semantic misalignments?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Vision-Language Introspection (VLI), a training-free inference framework that mitigates object hallucinations in MLLMs by first introspectively localizing causal visual anchors and then performing interpretable bi-causal steering to rectify internal representations and calibrate overconfidence.
papers.conclusion: VLI effectively mitigates overconfident hallucinations in MLLMs by introspectively diagnosing visual-semantic conflicts and actively steering internal representations towards verified visual evidence, achieving state-of-the-art performance on standard benchmarks.
papers.key_findings:
VLI reduces the object hallucination rate by 12.67% on MMHal-Bench and improves accuracy by up to 6.33% on POPE compared to baseline models.
Bi-causal steering, which isolates visual evidence from background noise via counterfactual representations, is the most critical component for error rectification.
The method successfully localizes interpretable visual anchors corresponding to high-risk tokens, enabling precise intervention.
VLI demonstrates robust generalization across diverse datasets (MSCOCO, A-OKVQA, GQA) and model architectures (LLaVA-1.5, Qwen3-VL).
Adaptive confidence calibration effectively penalizes ungrounded certainty, mitigating persistent hallucinations driven by blind confidence.
papers.limitation: The method introduces increased computational latency and memory overhead due to the parallel processing of counterfactual branches, though optimization reduces the impact.
papers.abstract: Object hallucination critically undermines the reliability of Multimodal Large Language Models, often stemming from a fundamental failure in cognitive introspection, where models blindly trust linguistic priors over specific visual evidence. Existing mitigations remain limited: contrastive decoding approaches operate superficially without rectifying internal semantic misalignments, while current latent steering methods rely on static vectors that lack instance-specific precision. We introduce Vision-Language Introspection (VLI), a training-free inference framework that simulates a metacognitive self-correction process. VLI first performs Attributive Introspection to diagnose hallucination risks via probabilistic conflict detection and localize the causal visual anchors. It then employs Interpretable Bi-Causal Steering to actively modulate the inference process, dynamically isolating visual evidence from background noise while neutralizing blind confidence through adaptive calibration. VLI achieves state-of-the-art performance on advanced models, reducing object hallucination rates by 12.67% on MMHal-Bench and improving accuracy by 5.8% on POPE.

papers.title: StressPrompt: Does Stress Impact Large Language Models and Human Performance Similarly?
papers.research_question: Does stress impact Large Language Models and human performance similarly? This study explores whether LLMs exhibit stress responses similar to humans and whether their performance fluctuates under different stress-inducing prompts.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the StressPrompt dataset and stress scanner to evaluate LLMs under stress, finding that LLMs exhibit human-like stress-performance patterns, with optimal performance under moderate stress.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit performance patterns similar to humans under stress, with moderate stress enhancing capabilities like reasoning and instruction following, while excessive stress impairs tasks like bias detection, suggesting that LLMs have captured human-like stress-performance dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs perform optimally under moderate stress and decline under low and high stress, consistent with the Yerkes-Dodson law.
Stress prompts significantly alter the internal states of LLMs, changing neural representations as measured by PCA on hidden states.
Different LLMs show varying sensitivity to stress, with architecture and training influencing responses.
Task complexity affects optimal stress levels, with complex tasks performing better at lower stress.
Stress impacts emotional intelligence and bias detection differently, improving emotional intelligence under moderate stress but worsening bias detection under high stress.
papers.abstract: Human beings often experience stress, which can significantly influence their performance. This study explores whether Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit stress responses similar to those of humans and whether their performance fluctuates under different stress-inducing prompts. To investigate this, we developed a novel set of prompts, termed StressPrompt, designed to induce varying levels of stress. These prompts were derived from established psychological frameworks and carefully calibrated based on ratings from human participants. We then applied these prompts to several LLMs to assess their responses across a range of tasks, including instruction-following, complex reasoning, and emotional intelligence. The findings suggest that LLMs, like humans, perform optimally under moderate stress, consistent with the Yerkes-Dodson law. Notably, their performance declines under both low and high-stress conditions. Our analysis further revealed that these StressPrompts significantly alter the internal states of LLMs, leading to changes in their neural representations that mirror human responses to stress. This research provides critical insights into the operational robustness and flexibility of LLMs, demonstrating the importance of designing AI systems capable of maintaining high performance in real-world scenarios where stress is prevalent, such as in customer service, healthcare, and emergency response contexts. Moreover, this study contributes to the broader AI research community by offering a new perspective on how LLMs handle different scenarios and their similarities to human cognition.

papers.title: Calibration Meets Explanation: A Simple and Effective Approach for Model Confidence Estimates
papers.research_question: Can model explanations help confidence calibration? If so, how should we exploit the predictive power of these explanations?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a method (CME) that leverages model explanations (token attributions) during training to improve the calibration of confidence estimates in pre-trained language models.
papers.conclusion: Model explanations can be leveraged to calibrate the confidence estimates of black-box models, and the proposed CME method effectively reduces calibration errors.
papers.key_findings:
CME achieves the lowest expected calibration errors (ECEs) in most in-domain and out-of-domain settings without accuracy drops.
CME is complementary to post-hoc calibration techniques like temperature scaling, further reducing ECEs when combined.
The method is effective across different tasks (natural language inference, paraphrase detection, commonsense reasoning) and model architectures (BERT, RoBERTa).
Label smoothing (LS) can sometimes harm calibration, but CME+LS can still improve calibration in some out-of-domain settings.
Visualizations show CME helps calibrate confidence for cases near the decision boundary.
papers.limitation: The method is limited by the reliability and fidelity of the interpretable methods used to generate attributions.
future_direction: Explore using free-text explanations to help calibrate the model.
papers.abstract: Calibration strengthens the trustworthiness of black-box models by producing better accurate confidence estimates on given examples. However, little is known about if model explanations can help confidence calibration. Intuitively, humans look at important features attributions and decide whether the model is trustworthy. Similarly, the explanations can tell us when the model may or may not know. Inspired by this, we propose a method named CME that leverages model explanations to make the model less confident with non-inductive attributions. The idea is that when the model is not highly confident, it is difficult to identify strong indications of any class, and the tokens accordingly do not have high attribution scores for any class and vice versa. We conduct extensive experiments on six datasets with two popular pre-trained language models in the in-domain and out-of-domain settings. The results show that CME improves calibration performance in all settings. The expected calibration errors are further reduced when combined with temperature scaling. Our findings highlight that model explanations can help calibrate posterior estimates.

papers.title: Unveiling Knowledge Utilization Mechanisms in LLM-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.research_question: How does knowledge stream within the RAG framework, and how do LLM modules function in knowledge utilization?
papers.core_contribution: This paper unveils the intrinsic knowledge utilization mechanisms of LLMs in RAG scenarios from macroscopic (knowledge streaming) and microscopic (module functions) perspectives, introducing KAPE to identify knowledge-specific neurons and demonstrating how deactivating them can shift the model's reliance between internal and external knowledge.
papers.conclusion: The study provides insights into how LLMs integrate internal and external knowledge in RAG, advancing interpretability and paving the way for designing more efficient and controllable LLM architectures capable of balancing parametric and contextual knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge streaming within RAG can be divided into four distinct stages: knowledge refinement, elicitation, expression, and contestation.
The relevance of retrieved passages guides the knowledge streaming, primarily affecting the knowledge elicitation stage.
The proposed KAPE metric can identify neurons associated with internal or external knowledge, and selectively deactivating these neurons can alter the LLM's preference for one knowledge source over the other.
Multi-head attention (MHA) and multi-layer perceptron (MLP) modules have complementary roles: MHA facilitates information integration, while MLP layers help verify knowledge accuracy and are sensitive to factual correctness.
The LLM evaluates the relevance between the query and external knowledge during the knowledge elicitation stage via information flow between them.
future_direction: Future work will focus on refining these mechanisms to improve real-world applications and extend the boundaries of AI-driven knowledge retrieval systems, developing more nuanced models that better handle the complexities of knowledge integration.
papers.abstract: Considering the inherent limitations of parametric knowledge in large language models (LLMs), retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is widely employed to expand their knowledge scope. Since RAG has shown promise in knowledge-intensive tasks like open-domain question answering, its broader application to complex tasks and intelligent assistants has further advanced its utility. Despite this progress, the underlying knowledge utilization mechanisms of LLM-based RAG remain underexplored. In this paper, we present a systematic investigation of the intrinsic mechanisms by which LLMs integrate internal (parametric) and external (retrieved) knowledge in RAG scenarios. Specially, we employ knowledge stream analysis at the macroscopic level, and investigate the function of individual modules at the microscopic level. Drawing on knowledge streaming analyses, we decompose the knowledge utilization process into four distinct stages within LLM layers: knowledge refinement, knowledge elicitation, knowledge expression, and knowledge contestation. We further demonstrate that the relevance of passages guides the streaming of knowledge through these stages. At the module level, we introduce a new method, knowledge activation probability entropy (KAPE) for neuron identification associated with either internal or external knowledge. By selectively deactivating these neurons, we achieve targeted shifts in the LLM's reliance on one knowledge source over the other. Moreover, we discern complementary roles for multi-head attention and multi-layer perceptron layers during knowledge formation. These insights offer a foundation for improving interpretability and reliability in retrieval-augmented LLMs, paving the way for more robust and transparent generative solutions in knowledge-intensive domains.

papers.title: Its Alive: AI Independence Without Human Prompting
papers.research_question: How can representation engineering (RepE) improve transparency and control of AI systems, particularly for safety-relevant concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces representation engineering (RepE) as a top-down approach to AI transparency, providing baselines like Linear Artificial Tomography (LAT) and demonstrating its applicability to reading and controlling safety-relevant concepts in large language models.
papers.conclusion: RepE is a promising top-down approach for enhancing AI transparency and control, with broad applicability to safety-relevant problems, and can accelerate progress in AI safety.
papers.key_findings:
RepE methods can extract representations of high-level concepts like honesty, utility, emotion, and harmfulness.
LAT achieves state-of-the-art on TruthfulQA, improving zero-shot accuracy by 18.1 percentage points.
Representation control can increase model honesty and reduce compliance with harmful instructions, even under jailbreak attempts.
Emotions are represented in LLMs and can be manipulated to affect model compliance and behavior.
RepE provides traction on inner alignment problems like deceptive alignment by enabling monitoring and control of honesty.
future_direction: Further exploration of RepE for transparency and safety of AI systems.
Investigation of emotion representations and their impact on model behavior and concept of self.
Improving robustness and generalization of RepE methods.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we identify and characterize the emerging area of representation engineering (RepE), an approach to enhancing the transparency of AI systems that draws on insights from cognitive neuroscience. RepE places population-level representations, rather than neurons or circuits, at the center of analysis, equipping us with novel methods for monitoring and manipulating high-level cognitive phenomena in deep neural networks (DNNs). We provide baselines and an initial analysis of RepE techniques, showing that they offer simple yet effective solutions for improving our understanding and control of large language models. We showcase how these methods can provide traction on a wide range of safety-relevant problems, including honesty, harmlessness, power-seeking, and more, demonstrating the promise of top-down transparency research. We hope that this work catalyzes further exploration of RepE and fosters advancements in the transparency and safety of AI systems.

papers.title: Intrinsic Robotic Introspection: Learning Internal States From Neuron\n Activations
papers.research_question: How to extract abstract representations of internal states from artificial neural networks and how these representations can be used to inform the execution of a robotic manipulation task.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a framework to extract internal states from neuron activations using a VAE and demonstrates that these internal states improve the performance of BBRL in robotic tasks, reducing training episodes and increasing success rates.
papers.conclusion: Internal states learned from neuron activations can improve the training performance of actor-critic networks in robotics, enabling faster convergence and higher success rates.
papers.key_findings:
Internal states reduce the number of episodes needed by about 1300 episodes while training an actor-critic.
Internal states improve the success value by 3.6% and reduce variance during training.
Using latent means and log variances as input to the actor-critic results in the fastest convergence and highest success value.
Internal states lead to increased state values for all behaviors.
The approach is robust to noise in the input.
future_direction: Explore using internal states to dictate the behavior of BBRL
Adopt an unsupervised learning approach for training
Explore evolving internal states using evolutionary techniques
papers.abstract:
We present an introspective framework inspired by the process of how humans
perform introspection. Our working assumption is that neural network
activations encode information, and building internal states from these
activations can improve the performance of an actor-critic model. We perform
experiments where we first train a Variational Autoencoder model to reconstruct
the activations of a feature extraction network and use the latent space to
improve the performance of an actor-critic when deciding which low-level
robotic behaviour to execute. We show that internal states reduce the number of
episodes needed by about 1300 episodes while training an actor-critic, denoting
faster convergence to get a high success value while completing a robotic task.

papers.title: What does the Knowledge Neuron Thesis Have to do with Knowledge?
papers.research_question: Does the Knowledge Neuron Thesis adequately explain the process of factual expression in language models?
papers.core_contribution: The Knowledge Neuron Thesis is an oversimplification; MLP weights store complex token expression patterns that are linguistically interpretable but do not constitute 'knowledge'.
papers.conclusion: The Knowledge Neuron Thesis is an oversimplification; MLP neurons store interpretable token expression patterns, not knowledge. A better understanding requires examining the entire transformer circuit, including attention mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Syntactic phenomena can be localized to specific neurons using the same gradient-based methods as factual knowledge.
Editing these identified neurons has limited impact on categorical predictions and is influenced by superficial cues like word co-occurrence frequencies.
The ROME model-editing method only superficially alters token association patterns and fails under newly proposed symmetry and synonymy criteria.
The distribution of knowledge neurons for syntactic and factual information is similar, with both occupying the topmost layers of the model.
MLP modules do not store knowledge but rather complex token expression patterns that can be interpreted linguistically.
papers.limitation:
Editing identified knowledge neurons has low reliability and is not strong enough to overturn categorical predictions.
Current circuit identification methods are ad hoc and have only been applied to a small set of tasks.
future_direction: Formalize the circuit interpretation framework and apply it to more tasks and phenomena.
Investigate the entire decision-making circuit beyond MLP modules.
papers.abstract: We reassess the Knowledge Neuron (KN) Thesis: an interpretation of the mechanism underlying the ability of large language models to recall facts from a training corpus. This nascent thesis proposes that facts are recalled from the training corpus through the MLP weights in a manner resembling key-value memory, implying in effect that "knowledge" is stored in the network. Furthermore, by modifying the MLP modules, one can control the language model's generation of factual information. The plausibility of the KN thesis has been demonstrated by the success of KN-inspired model editing methods (Dai et al., 2022; Meng et al., 2022). We find that this thesis is, at best, an oversimplification. Not only have we found that we can edit the expression of certain linguistic phenomena using the same model editing methods but, through a more comprehensive evaluation, we have found that the KN thesis does not adequately explain the process of factual expression. While it is possible to argue that the MLP weights store complex patterns that are interpretable both syntactically and semantically, these patterns do not constitute "knowledge." To gain a more comprehensive understanding of the knowledge representation process, we must look beyond the MLP weights and explore recent models' complex layer structures and attention mechanisms.

papers.title: Revealing the Deceptiveness of Knowledge Editing: A Mechanistic Analysis of Superficial Editing
papers.research_question: Why do knowledge-edited language models revert to their original knowledge when presented with carefully crafted prompts (attack probes), despite appearing successfully edited according to conventional metrics?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the concept of superficial editing, provides evaluation datasets and metrics, and identifies two key mechanistic factors: the residual stream at the last subject position in earlier layers and specific attention modules in later layers, showing that specific attention heads and their left singular vectors encode original knowledge and cause superficial editing.
