papers.conclusion: Superficial editing is a significant challenge for knowledge editing, and the mechanistic analysis reveals the underlying factors in the residual stream and attention modules, with broader applicability to unlearning tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Existing knowledge editing algorithms achieve near-perfect conventional metrics but are vulnerable to attack probes, exhibiting superficial editing in over 70% of cases for some methods.
The residual stream at the last subject position in earlier layers shows inhibited enrichment of new knowledge and limited accumulation of original knowledge.
Later attention modules cause the Reversal of the Residual Stream (RRS) phenomenon by incorporating original knowledge into the last position, leading to superficial editing.
Specific attention heads in later layers and their left singular vectors are causally responsible for encoding original knowledge and inducing superficial editing.
Similar patterns are observed in superficial unlearning, demonstrating the generality of the findings.
papers.abstract: Knowledge editing, which aims to update the knowledge encoded in language models, can be deceptive. Despite the fact that many existing knowledge editing algorithms achieve near-perfect performance on conventional metrics, the models edited by them are still prone to generating original knowledge. This paper introduces the concept of "superficial editing" to describe this phenomenon. Our comprehensive evaluation reveals that this issue presents a significant challenge to existing algorithms. Through systematic investigation, we identify and validate two key factors contributing to this issue: (1) the residual stream at the last subject position in earlier layers and (2) specific attention modules in later layers. Notably, certain attention heads in later layers, along with specific left singular vectors in their output matrices, encapsulate the original knowledge and exhibit a causal relationship with superficial editing. Furthermore, we extend our analysis to the task of superficial unlearning, where we observe consistent patterns in the behavior of specific attention heads and their corresponding left singular vectors, thereby demonstrating the robustness and broader applicability of our methodology and conclusions. Our code is available here.

papers.title: Loop as a Bridge: Can Looped Transformers Truly Link Representation Space and Natural Language Outputs?
papers.research_question: Can Looped Transformers align linguistic verification output with representations? Can LTs enhance their introspective awareness on representations?
papers.core_contribution: Increasing loop iterations in Looped Transformers narrows the gap between self-verification and representation readout, but partly due to degradation of representation quality. Moreover, LTs only show introspective awareness in the final loop, not continuously across loops.
papers.conclusion: Current Looped Transformers do not yet achieve continuous introspection across loops, and the observed gap narrowing is partly driven by a degradation in representation quality.
papers.key_findings:
The accuracy of textual self-verification improves with more loop iterations.
The performance of representation-based linear probes declines with more loop iterations.
The gap between representation readout and self-verification narrows with more loops, but partly because of the decline in representation readout.
LTs are only aware of injected concepts when the injection occurs in the final loop, not in earlier loops.
papers.limitation: The experiments are a preliminary exploration conducted on a single specific implementation of LTs (Ouro), so the observed limitations should not be interpreted as intrinsic flaws of the general LTs paradigm.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often exhibit a gap between their internal knowledge and their explicit linguistic outputs. In this report, we empirically investigate whether Looped Transformers (LTs)--architectures that increase computational depth by iterating shared layers--can bridge this gap by utilizing their iterative nature as a form of introspection. Our experiments reveal that while increasing loop iterations narrows the gap, it is partly driven by a degradation of their internal knowledge carried by representations. Moreover, another empirical analysis suggests that current LTs' ability to perceive representations does not improve across loops; it is only present in the final loop. These results suggest that while LTs offer a promising direction for scaling computational depth, they have yet to achieve the introspection required to truly link representation space and natural language.

papers.title: The Curious Case of Analogies: Investigating Analogical Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode and apply high-level relational concepts for analogical reasoning, and how do they structurally align analogous situations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper investigates the internal mechanisms of analogical reasoning in LLMs, finding that they encode relational information in mid-upper layers but struggle to apply it, and that successful reasoning is associated with strong structural alignment between analogous situations.
papers.conclusion: LLMs show emerging but limited capabilities in analogical reasoning, with parallels to human cognition in encoding relational information and structural alignment, but gaps in application and alignment.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs effectively encode underlying relationships between analogous entities in mid-upper layers, with relational information being a key factor for correct reasoning.
LLMs struggle not only when relational information is missing but also when attempting to apply it to new entities.
Strategically patching hidden representations at critical token positions can facilitate information transfer and improve performance.
Successful analogical reasoning is marked by strong structural alignment between analogous situations, while failures show degraded alignment.
Analogical structure becomes linearly separable in middle layers, and token-level alignment (measured by Mutual Alignment Score) is higher for correct analogies.
future_direction: Future research into understanding and improving the analogical reasoning capabilities of LLMs.
papers.abstract: Analogical reasoning is at the core of human cognition, serving as an important foundation for a variety of intellectual activities. While prior work has shown that LLMs can represent task patterns and surface-level concepts, it remains unclear whether these models can encode high-level relational concepts and apply them to novel situations through structured comparisons. In this work, we explore this fundamental aspect using proportional and story analogies, and identify three key findings. First, LLMs effectively encode the underlying relationships between analogous entities; both attributive and relational information propagate through mid-upper layers in correct cases, whereas reasoning failures reflect missing relational information within these layers. Second, unlike humans, LLMs often struggle not only when relational information is missing, but also when attempting to apply it to new entities. In such cases, strategically patching hidden representations at critical token positions can facilitate information transfer to a certain extent. Lastly, successful analogical reasoning in LLMs is marked by strong structural alignment between analogous situations, whereas failures often reflect degraded or misplaced alignment. Overall, our findings reveal that LLMs exhibit emerging but limited capabilities in encoding and applying high-level relational concepts, highlighting both parallels and gaps with human cognition.

papers.title: All Bark and No Bite: Rogue Dimensions in Transformer Language Models Obscure Representational Quality
papers.research_question: How informative are standard similarity measures (cosine similarity, Euclidean distance) in contextualized language models, and how do rogue dimensions dominate these measures, obscuring representational quality?
papers.core_contribution: Standard similarity measures in contextual language models are dominated by a small number of rogue dimensions, and simple postprocessing techniques like standardization can correct for this, revealing underlying representational quality that is preserved across all layers.
papers.conclusion: Standard similarity measures are not informative for contextual language models due to rogue dimensions, and accounting for these dimensions (e.g., via standardization) is essential for any similarity-based analysis.
papers.key_findings:
A small number of rogue dimensions (1-5) dominate cosine similarity and Euclidean distance in contextual language models.
Rogue dimensions are centered far from the origin and have disproportionately high variance.
The rogue dimensions that dominate similarity measures do not dominate model behavior; ablating them has little effect on the language modeling distribution.
Rogue dimensions are often correlated with specific tokens (e.g., punctuation) and positions (e.g., position zero).
After postprocessing (e.g., standardization), representational quality (correlation with human similarity judgments) improves and is preserved across all layers, contrary to previous claims of degradation in later layers.
future_direction: Designing and implementing language models that do not develop rogue dimensions in the first place.
Understanding how rogue dimensions arise over time during pretraining.
Using the MultiBERT checkpoints to study whether rogue dimensions are coincidental or requisite for good performance, and how they emerge.
papers.abstract: Similarity measures are a vital tool for understanding how language models represent and process language. Standard representational similarity measures such as cosine similarity and Euclidean distance have been successfully used in static word embedding models to understand how words cluster in semantic space. Recently, these measures have been applied to embeddings from contextualized models such as BERT and GPT-2. In this work, we call into question the informativity of such measures for contextualized language models. We find that a small number of rogue dimensions, often just 1-3, dominate these measures. Moreover, we find a striking mismatch between the dimensions that dominate similarity measures and those which are important to the behavior of the model. We show that simple postprocessing techniques such as standardization are able to correct for rogue dimensions and reveal underlying representational quality. We argue that accounting for rogue dimensions is essential for any similarity-based analysis of contextual language models.

papers.title: Exploring Concept Depth: How Large Language Models Acquire Knowledge and Concept at Different Layers?
papers.research_question: Can shallow layers in LLMs capture meaningful features of simple knowledge, while complex concepts need deeper layers to capture their meaningful features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the concept of 'Concept Depth' to measure how different layers in LLMs capture concepts of varying complexity, showing that simpler concepts are learned in shallow layers while complex concepts require deeper layers.
papers.conclusion: The Concept Depth metric provides a useful framework for understanding how LLMs process concepts of varying complexity across layers, and the experimental insights enhance the understanding of internal representations in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Simpler concepts (e.g., factual knowledge) are learned in shallow layers, while more complex concepts (e.g., reasoning tasks) require deeper layers for accurate understanding.
The pattern of Concept Depth is consistent across different model families (Gemma, LLaMA, Qwen) and model sizes.
Larger models within a family tend to achieve higher peak accuracy and sometimes converge to optimal performance at earlier layers.
Adding noise to the input or quantizing model weights (e.g., to 8-bit) slows down the convergence of concept understanding, requiring deeper layers to achieve comparable accuracy.
Compressing models to 16-bit quantization does not significantly harm the understanding process compared to 32-bit.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable performances across a wide range of tasks. However, the mechanisms by which these models encode tasks of varying complexities remain poorly understood. In this paper, we explore the hypothesis that LLMs process concepts of varying complexities in different layers, introducing the idea of "Concept Depth" to suggest that more complex concepts are typically acquired in deeper layers. Specifically, we categorize concepts based on their level of abstraction, defining them in the order of increasing complexity within factual, emotional, and inferential tasks. We conduct extensive probing experiments using layer-wise representations across various LLM families (Gemma, LLaMA, Qwen) on various datasets spanning the three domains of tasks. Our findings reveal that models could efficiently conduct probing for simpler tasks in shallow layers, and more complex tasks typically necessitate deeper layers for accurate understanding. Additionally, we examine how external factors, such as adding noise to the input and quantizing the model weights, might affect layer-wise representations. Our findings suggest that these factors can impede the development of a conceptual understanding of LLMs until deeper layers are explored. We hope that our proposed concept and experimental insights will enhance the understanding of the mechanisms underlying LLMs. Our codes are available at https://github.com/Luckfort/CD.

papers.title: Language Models Represent Space and Time
papers.research_question: Do large language models learn coherent linear representations of space and time, i.e., do they form a world model?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models learn linear representations of space and time that are robust to prompting and unified across entity types, and individual 'space' and 'time' neurons exist that encode these coordinates.
papers.conclusion: Modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes can recover spatial and temporal coordinates from internal activations, with performance increasing with model size and plateauing in middle layers.
Spatial and temporal features are linearly represented, as nonlinear probes do not improve performance.
Representations are robust to variations in prompting, though random tokens or capitalization degrade performance.
Probes generalize across entity types and to held-out geographic or temporal blocks, indicating unified representations.
Individual neurons exist that are highly predictive of space and time, and causal interventions confirm their importance.
papers.limitation:
Data comes only from English Wikipedia, skewing towards the Anglosphere, and entity type distribution is not uniform.
The true extent and structure of spatial and temporal representations remain unclear.
future_direction: Extracting representations in the model’s coordinate system rather than human coordinates, e.g., with sparse autoencoders.
Studying how these spatiotemporal representations are learned, recalled, and used internally across training checkpoints.
Investigating potential parallels with biological place and grid cells in the brain.
papers.abstract: The capabilities of large language models (LLMs) have sparked debate over whether such systems just learn an enormous collection of superficial statistics or a set of more coherent and grounded representations that reflect the real world. We find evidence for the latter by analyzing the learned representations of three spatial datasets (world, US, NYC places) and three temporal datasets (historical figures, artworks, news headlines) in the Llama-2 family of models. We discover that LLMs learn linear representations of space and time across multiple scales. These representations are robust to prompting variations and unified across different entity types (e.g. cities and landmarks). In addition, we identify individual "space neurons" and "time neurons" that reliably encode spatial and temporal coordinates. While further investigation is needed, our results suggest modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.

papers.title: ReflCtrl: Controlling LLM Reflection via Representation Engineering
papers.research_question: When does the model initiate reflection during its reasoning process? How does reflection influence the model's reasoning performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces ReflCtrl, a representation engineering framework that extracts a reflection direction in the latent space to control self-reflection in reasoning LLMs, and shows that reflections are often redundant and can be reduced to save inference cost without sacrificing performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes ReflCtrl for controlling self-reflection in reasoning LLMs, demonstrates reflection redundancy and its connection to internal uncertainty, and shows that stepwise steering can reduce inference cost with minimal accuracy loss.
papers.key_findings:
Reflections are redundant, especially in stronger models, and up to 33.6% of reasoning tokens can be saved while preserving performance.
The model's reflection behavior is highly correlated with internal uncertainty signals, implying self-reflection may be controlled by model's uncertainty.
Stepwise steering can control reflection frequency and reduces performance loss compared to all-token steering.
The reflection direction can be used to predict answer correctness, suggesting it encodes uncertainty information.
Smaller models are more sensitive to reflection reduction than larger models.
papers.limitation:
Identification of reasoning steps relies on keyword search, which may be model specific.
ReflCtrl only works for open-source models and it remains unclear whether it generalizes to SOTA closed-source models such as GPT-4 or Claude.
future_direction: developing uncertainty-aware dynamic steering to adjust steering strength during inference
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning have achieved strong performance across diverse tasks, including mathematics, coding, and general reasoning. A distinctive ability of these reasoning models is self-reflection: the ability to review and revise previous reasoning steps. While self-reflection enhances reasoning performance, it also increases inference cost. In this work, we study self-reflection through the lens of representation engineering. We segment the model's reasoning into steps, identify the steps corresponding to reflection, and extract a reflection direction in the latent space that governs this behavior. Using this direction, we propose a stepwise steering method that can control reflection frequency. We call our framework ReflCtrl. Our experiments show that (1) in many cases reflections are redundant, especially in stronger models (in our experiments, we can save up to 33.6 percent of reasoning tokens while preserving performance), and (2) the model's reflection behavior is highly correlated with an internal uncertainty signal, implying self-reflection may be controlled by the model's uncertainty.

papers.title: Do Llamas Work in English? On the Latent Language of Multilingual Transformers
papers.research_question: Do multilingual language models trained on English-dominated corpora use English as an internal pivot language?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual transformers like Llama-2 use English as an internal pivot language, with intermediate layers representing concepts in English before mapping to the target language, indicating an English bias in their internal representations.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual LLMs have an English bias in their internal representations, which may lead to linguistic biases and has implications for equitable AI.
papers.key_findings:
In translation tasks, intermediate layers decode the English version of the correct next token before switching to the target language.
The forward pass goes through three phases: input space, concept space (biased towards English), and output space.
Token energy is low in middle layers, indicating that latents are in a concept space orthogonal to token space.
The English bias is less pronounced for languages with single-token words (like Chinese) in repetition tasks.
The same pattern is observed in Mistral-7B, suggesting generality of the phenomenon.
papers.limitation:
Focus on Llama-2 family, so claims may not generalize to other models.
Tasks are simple and controlled, not real-world.
Limited understanding of the concept space structure.
Logit lens only reveals part of the internal state.
future_direction: Investigate how English bias affects downstream model behavior.
Study how English bias changes with different training data or tokenizers.
Extend to a wider range of tasks and models.

papers.title: Knowledge Localization: Mission Not Accomplished? Enter Query Localization!
papers.research_question: Does the Knowledge Localization (KL) assumption hold for all facts? If not, what is a more realistic assumption?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes the Query Localization (QL) assumption, which includes query-KN mapping and dynamic KN selection, and introduces a Consistency-Aware KN modification method that improves knowledge editing performance.
papers.conclusion: The Query Localization assumption provides a more realistic framework for understanding knowledge storage and expression in LLMs than the Knowledge Localization assumption, and is validated by improved editing performance.
papers.key_findings:
Inconsistent Knowledge (KI) that violates the Knowledge Localization assumption is widespread in LLMs.
For KI, knowledge neurons are associated with specific queries rather than the fact itself (query-KN mapping).
The attention module plays a key role in selecting appropriate knowledge neurons for expression (dynamic KN selection).
The proposed Consistency-Aware KN modification method, based on the QL assumption, improves knowledge editing performance over baseline methods.
papers.limitation:
The work primarily focuses on factual knowledge, and it remains unclear whether the QL assumption applies to other types of knowledge.
The distinction between Consistent Knowledge (KC) and Inconsistent Knowledge (KI) might be related to the pre-training process.
future_direction: Exploring how to reconcile the QL assumption with other current theories.
Further utilizing the QL assumption to improve model editing methods.
Integrating the attention module more effectively to develop enhanced methods for dynamically editing knowledge.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) store extensive factual knowledge, but the mechanisms behind how they store and express this knowledge remain unclear. The Knowledge Neuron (KN) thesis is a prominent theory for explaining these mechanisms. This theory is based on the Knowledge Localization (KL) assumption, which suggests that a fact can be localized to a few knowledge storage units, namely knowledge neurons. However, this assumption has two limitations: first, it may be too rigid regarding knowledge storage, and second, it neglects the role of the attention module in knowledge expression. In this paper, we first re-examine the KL assumption and demonstrate that its limitations do indeed exist. To address these, we then present two new findings, each targeting one of the limitations: one focusing on knowledge storage and the other on knowledge expression. We summarize these findings as \textbf{Query Localization} (QL) assumption and argue that the KL assumption can be viewed as a simplification of the QL assumption. Based on QL assumption, we further propose the Consistency-Aware KN modification method, which improves the performance of knowledge modification, further validating our new assumption. We conduct 39 sets of experiments, along with additional visualization experiments, to rigorously confirm our conclusions. Code is available at https://github.com/heng840/KnowledgeLocalization.

papers.title: Toward Better Generalisation in Uncertainty Estimators: Leveraging Data-Agnostic Features
papers.research_question: Can supplementing hidden-state features with data-agnostic features improve the probe’s generalisation to unseen tasks or datasets? Does pruning to the top-ranked hidden-state features amplify this generalisation?
papers.core_contribution: This paper investigates whether incorporating data-agnostic features (probability- and entropy-based metrics) with hidden-state features improves the generalization of uncertainty estimators across tasks and datasets, and whether feature selection on hidden states amplifies this effect.
papers.conclusion: Integrating data-agnostic features with hidden-state features can enhance the generalization of uncertainty estimators, and feature selection can amplify this effect, but the approach underperforms on certain transfer pairs, particularly involving Commonsense Reasoning datasets, where the probe fails to prioritize the data-agnostic features.
papers.key_findings:
Incorporating data-agnostic features generally improves generalization performance, especially for short-form question answering datasets, but fails in some cases involving Commonsense Reasoning datasets.
Feature selection (retaining top-k hidden-state features) can amplify the contribution of data-agnostic features and yield additional gains, but the expected ordering of improvement does not always hold.
Analysis using SHAP values reveals that in successful cases, data-agnostic features are highly ranked, but in failure cases (e.g., with SWAG and Winogrande datasets) they are underweighted or sparsely ranked.
Probes trained solely on hidden-state features generalize poorly across tasks and datasets, indicating overfitting to dataset-specific features.
Factual QA and Reading Comprehension tasks show better cross-generalization, likely because their hidden-state representations are more similar, as suggested by PCA visualization.
papers.limitation:
The data-agnostic features were randomly selected without investigating whether all are effective or if including more/less would affect performance.
The rate of correct answers being misclassified when incorporating data-agnostic features is relatively high.
The baseline (without data-agnostic features) drifts slightly across the three probe configurations, introducing instability in comparisons.
The probe underweights data-agnostic features in Commonsense Reasoning datasets, suggesting their hidden states may already encode similar information.
future_direction: Systematically examine the effectiveness of individual data-agnostic features and the impact of including more or less of them.
Investigate the high rate of correct answers being misclassified when data-agnostic features are added.
Compare the proposed accuracy probe with the semantic entropy probe for generalization performance.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often generate responses that are factually incorrect yet expressed with high confidence, which can pose serious risks for end users. To address this, it is essential for LLMs not only to produce answers but also to provide accurate estimates of their correctness. Uncertainty quantification methods have been introduced to assess the quality of LLM outputs, with factual accuracy being a key aspect of that quality. Among these methods, those that leverage hidden states to train probes have shown particular promise, as these internal representations encode information relevant to the factuality of responses, making this approach the focus of this paper. However, the probe trained on the hidden states of one dataset often struggles to generalise to another dataset of a different task or domain. To address this limitation, we explore combining data-agnostic features with hidden-state features and assess whether this hybrid feature set enhances out-of-domain performance. We further examine whether selecting only the most informative hidden-state features, thereby discarding task-specific noise, enables the data-agnostic features to contribute more effectively. The experiment results indicate that although introducing data-agnostic features generally enhances generalisation performance in most cases, in certain scenarios their inclusion degrades performance. A similar pattern emerges when retaining only the most important hidden-state features - adding data-agnostic features does not consistently further enhance performance compared to using the full set of hidden-state features. A closer analysis reveals that, in some specific cases, the trained probe underweights the data-agnostic features relative to the hidden-state features, which we believe is the main reason why the results are inconclusive.

papers.title: Identifying Semantic Induction Heads to Understand In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether attention heads in transformers encode semantic relationships (syntactic dependencies and knowledge graph relations) and how the formation of such semantic induction heads correlates with the emergence of in-context learning abilities.
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers semantic induction heads in transformers that encode semantic relationships and shows their emergence correlates with the development of in-context learning abilities.
papers.conclusion: The study of semantic induction heads advances understanding of attention head operations and provides insights into the in-context learning of LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads in transformers encode syntactic dependencies (subj, obj, mod) and semantic relationships from knowledge graphs.
The model's ability to understand dependencies is reflected in attention heads, with some heads specializing in specific relations.
In-context learning emerges progressively in three levels: loss reduction, format compliance, and pattern discovery.
The formation of semantic induction heads coincides with the emergence of pattern discovery in ICL.
Semantic induction heads are crucial for the model's ability to perform in-context learning.
papers.abstract: Although large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance, the lack of transparency in their inference logic raises concerns about their trustworthiness. To gain a better understanding of LLMs, we conduct a detailed analysis of the operations of attention heads and aim to better understand the in-context learning of LLMs. Specifically, we investigate whether attention heads encode two types of relationships between tokens present in natural languages: the syntactic dependency parsed from sentences and the relation within knowledge graphs. We find that certain attention heads exhibit a pattern where, when attending to head tokens, they recall tail tokens and increase the output logits of those tail tokens. More crucially, the formulation of such semantic induction heads has a close correlation with the emergence of the in-context learning ability of language models. The study of semantic attention heads advances our understanding of the intricate operations of attention heads in transformers, and further provides new insights into the in-context learning of LLMs.

papers.title: Measuring and Analyzing Intelligence via Contextual Uncertainty in Large Language Models using Information-Theoretic Metrics
papers.research_question: How do large language models process information as context length grows? The paper investigates this by building a quantitative Cognitive Profile for any model using information-theoretic metrics.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a task-agnostic method for building a quantitative Cognitive Profile of LLMs by tracking predictive uncertainty (via the Entropy Decay Curve) and summarizing it with the Information Gain Span, which reveals how models process information and can detect memorization.
papers.conclusion: The Entropy Decay Curve and Information Gain Span offer a principled, task-agnostic way to analyze and compare the internal dynamics of LLMs, revealing differences in how models process information and flagging potential memorization.
papers.key_findings:
Larger models (like Llama 3.3 70.6B) show a sharper decline in uncertainty with context length compared to smaller models.
The Entropy Decay Curve (EDC) is corpus-dependent: easier texts (like Alice's Adventures in Wonderland) lead to lower long-context uncertainty than more complex texts (like Ulysses and Kant's Critique of Judgement).
The EDC can detect memorization (entropy collapse) when long-context uncertainty becomes extremely low, indicating potential data contamination.
The Information Gain Span (IGS) provides a single scalar that summarizes the desirability of the decay pattern (high initial uncertainty and low final uncertainty).
The method provides a quantitative way to compare models and texts without task-specific benchmarks.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to a small set of models, corpora, and window lengths, and relies on finite-sample Monte Carlo estimates.
future_direction: Extend coverage to more architectures and training regimes.
Evaluate specialized domains (code, scientific, medical, legal).
Characterize estimator variance and sensitivity to sampling design, and refine contamination tests by combining EDC signals with independent memorization audits.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) excel on many task-specific benchmarks, yet the mechanisms that drive this success remain poorly understood. We move from asking what these systems can do to asking how they process information. Our contribution is a task-agnostic method that builds a quantitative Cognitive Profile for any model. The profile is built around the Entropy Decay Curve -- a plot of a model's normalised predictive uncertainty as context length grows. Across several state-of-the-art LLMs and diverse texts, the curves expose distinctive, stable profiles that depend on both model scale and text complexity. We also propose the Information Gain Span (IGS) as a single index that summarises the desirability of a decay pattern. Together, these tools offer a principled way to analyse and compare the internal dynamics of modern AI systems.

papers.title: Calibrating Verbal Uncertainty as a Linear Feature to Reduce Hallucinations
papers.research_question: How is verbal uncertainty represented in LLMs, and can calibrating it with semantic uncertainty detect and mitigate hallucinations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that verbal uncertainty in LLMs is mediated by a linear feature (VUF) and introduces Mechanistic Uncertainty Calibration (MUC) to calibrate verbal uncertainty with semantic uncertainty, reducing confident hallucinations by ~30%.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that verbal uncertainty is a linear feature in LLMs, and calibrating it with semantic uncertainty through MUC effectively reduces confident hallucinations, making LLMs more trustworthy.
papers.key_findings:
Verbal uncertainty in LLMs is governed by a single linear direction (VUF) in the representation space, extractable via difference-in-means.
The mismatch between semantic and verbal uncertainty is a better predictor of hallucinations than semantic uncertainty alone.
Inference-time intervention on VUF (MUC) calibrates verbal uncertainty with semantic uncertainty, reducing confident hallucinations by an average of 29.6% in short-form QA tasks.
VUFs are consistent across different datasets and models, indicating a universal feature.
MUC improves the alignment between verbal and semantic uncertainty, as shown by increased correlation coefficients.
papers.limitation: The method may reduce correctness rate due to noise in semantic uncertainty measurement, leading to unnecessary abstentions.
papers.abstract: LLMs often adopt an assertive language style also when making false claims. Such ``overconfident hallucinations'' mislead users and erode trust. Achieving the ability to express in language the actual degree of uncertainty around a claim is therefore of great importance. We find that ``verbal uncertainty'' is governed by a single linear feature in the representation space of LLMs, and show that this has only moderate correlation with the actual ``semantic uncertainty'' of the model. We apply this insight and show that (1) the mismatch between semantic and verbal uncertainty is a better predictor of hallucinations than semantic uncertainty alone and (2) we can intervene on verbal uncertainty at inference time and reduce confident hallucinations on short-form answers, achieving an average relative reduction of ~30%.

papers.title: Decoupling Knowledge and Reasoning in LLMs: An Exploration Using Cognitive Dual-System Theory
papers.research_question: How can the contributions of knowledge retrieval and reasoning adjustment be separated and quantified in large language models during inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a cognition attribution framework based on dual-system theory to decouple knowledge and reasoning in LLMs, revealing domain-specific reasoning benefits, scaling effects, and a hierarchical separation of knowledge (lower layers) and reasoning (higher layers).
papers.conclusion: The proposed cognition attribution architecture offers a novel perspective for understanding LLM cognition and provides insights into scaling laws, hierarchical knowledge editing, and the reasoning limitations of small models.
papers.key_findings:
Reasoning adjustment is domain-specific, benefiting reasoning-intensive domains (e.g., mathematics, physics, chemistry) and potentially impairing knowledge-intensive domains.
Parameter scaling improves both knowledge and reasoning, with knowledge improvements being more pronounced. Scaling also makes reasoning significantly more prudent (reduces overthinking) and modestly more intelligent (increases correction) in specific domains.
Knowledge retrieval primarily occurs in lower network layers, while reasoning adjustments are localized in higher layers, suggesting a functional separation.
Small LLMs tend to overthink more than they correct during reasoning, leading to negative or limited reasoning gains.
LLMs exhibit a human-like anchoring effect, which reasoning adjustment helps to mitigate.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation is limited to multiple-choice QA; future work should extend to open-ended generation.
The study does not include ultra-large models (>100B parameters).
The methods are simplified and may not fully capture the underlying mechanisms in LLMs.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to open-ended generation tasks.
Include ultra-large models (>100B parameters) in the study.
Conduct a more in-depth exploration of the phenomena observed using the framework.
papers.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) leverage both knowledge and reasoning during inference, the capacity to distinguish between them plays a pivotal role in model analysis, interpretability, and development. Inspired by dual-system cognitive theory, we propose a cognition attribution framework to decouple the contribution of knowledge and reasoning. In particular, the cognition of LLMs is decomposed into two distinct yet complementary phases: knowledge retrieval (Phase 1) and reasoning adjustment (Phase 2). To separate these phases, LLMs are prompted to generate answers under two different cognitive modes, fast thinking and slow thinking, respectively. The performance under different cognitive modes is analyzed to quantify the contribution of knowledge and reasoning. This architecture is employed to 15 LLMs across 3 datasets. Results reveal: (1) reasoning adjustment is domain-specific, benefiting reasoning-intensive domains (e.g., mathematics, physics, and chemistry) and potentially imparing knowledge-intensive domains. (2) Parameter scaling improves both knowledge and reasoning, with knowledge improvements being more pronounced. Additionally, parameter scaling make LLMs reasoning significantly more prudent, while moderately more intelligent. (3) Knowledge primarily resides in lower network layers, while reasoning operates in higher layers. Our framework not only helps understand LLMs from a "decoupling" perspective, but also provides new insights into existing research, including scaling laws, hierarchical knowledge editing, and limitations of small-model reasoning.

papers.title: Characterizing Mechanisms for Factual Recall in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do distributional and mechanistic factors determine a language model's behavior when there is a conflict between memorized facts and in-context information?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies specific attention heads that control the use of memorized vs. in-context information and shows that scaling these heads at runtime can dynamically control model behavior without parameter updates.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that frequency and specific attention heads influence factual recall and provides a proof of concept for controlling model behavior dynamically at runtime.
papers.key_findings:
The frequency of the country and in-context city in pretraining data affects the model's tendency to use memorized vs. in-context information.
Larger models are more likely to use memorized answers, especially for frequent terms.
Individual attention heads can be identified that promote either memorized or in-context answers.
Scaling down a memory head can increase the rate of in-context answers to 88% on the world capitals task.
The memory head promotes geography-related tokens, indicating domain specificity, and does not generalize well to other factual domains.
papers.limitation: The dataset used is templated and limited to the domain of country-capital relationships, so findings may not generalize to arbitrary contexts.
future_direction: Developing more general techniques for controlling the use of context vs. memorized information in arbitrary tasks.
Discovering more general mechanisms beyond domain-specific heads.
papers.abstract: Language Models (LMs) often must integrate facts they memorized in pretraining with new information that appears in a given context. These two sources can disagree, causing competition within the model, and it is unclear how an LM will resolve the conflict. On a dataset that queries for knowledge of world capitals, we investigate both distributional and mechanistic determinants of LM behavior in such situations. Specifically, we measure the proportion of the time an LM will use a counterfactual prefix (e.g., “The capital of Poland is London”) to overwrite what it learned in pretraining (“Warsaw”). On Pythia and GPT2, the training frequency of both the query country (”Poland”) and the in-context city (”London”) highly affect the models’ likelihood of using the counterfactual. We then use head attribution to identify individual attention heads that either promote the memorized answer or the in-context answer in the logits. By scaling up or down the value vector of these heads, we can control the likelihood of using the in-context answer on new data. This method can increase the rate of generating the in-context answer to 88% of the time simply by scaling a single head at runtime. Our work contributes to a body of evidence showing that we can often localize model behaviors to specific components and provides a proof of concept for how future methods might control model behavior dynamically at runtime.

papers.title: Inference-Time Intervention: Eliciting Truthful Answers from a Language Model
papers.research_question: How can we enhance the truthfulness of large language models by intervening on their activations during inference?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Inference-Time Intervention (ITI), a minimally invasive technique that shifts activations along truthful directions in attention heads during inference to improve model truthfulness.
papers.conclusion: ITI is a promising, efficient method for improving truthfulness in LLMs, suggesting that models internally represent truth which can be elicited through activation shifts.
papers.key_findings:
ITI significantly improves truthfulness on the TruthfulQA benchmark, e.g., increasing Alpaca's truthfulness from 32.5% to 65.1%.
There is a trade-off between truthfulness and helpfulness that can be balanced by tuning intervention strength.
ITI is data-efficient, requiring only a few hundred examples to find truthful directions.
ITI generalizes to other question-answering benchmarks (Natural Questions, TriviaQA, MMLU) with smaller improvements.
LLMs appear to have an internal representation of truth even when generating falsehoods.
papers.limitation:
ITI is not sufficient for ensuring truthful answers from LLMs and should be part of a more comprehensive approach.
There is a trade-off between truthfulness and helpfulness; increasing truthfulness may reduce informativeness.
future_direction: Test ITI on a wider variety of benchmarks beyond TruthfulQA.
Investigate the mechanistic understanding of what ITI does to internal representations.
papers.abstract: We introduce Inference-Time Intervention (ITI), a technique designed to enhance the "truthfulness" of large language models (LLMs). ITI operates by shifting model activations during inference, following a set of directions across a limited number of attention heads. This intervention significantly improves the performance of LLaMA models on the TruthfulQA benchmark. On an instruction-finetuned LLaMA called Alpaca, ITI improves its truthfulness from 32.5% to 65.1%. We identify a tradeoff between truthfulness and helpfulness and demonstrate how to balance it by tuning the intervention strength. ITI is minimally invasive and computationally inexpensive. Moreover, the technique is data efficient: while approaches like RLHF require extensive annotations, ITI locates truthful directions using only few hundred examples. Our findings suggest that LLMs may have an internal representation of the likelihood of something being true, even as they produce falsehoods on the surface.

papers.title: Blackbox meets blackbox: Representational Similarity and Stability Analysis of Neural Language Models and Brains
papers.research_question: How sensitive are neural language model representations to prior context, and how do these representations compare to human brain activations during story reading?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Representational Stability Analysis (ReStA) to analyze context-dependence in neural language models, finding that LSTM-based models are more similar to brain representations than transformer-based models, and that deeper layers are more context-dependent.
papers.conclusion: ReStA and RSA are useful for comparing models and brains, but caution is required due to low correlations. LSTM-based models are more similar to brain data, and brain data may only reflect shallow linguistic processing.
papers.key_findings:
LSTM-based models (GoogleLM and ELMO) show higher similarity between their two layers compared to BERT.
For LSTM-based models, the first layer is less sensitive to context length than the last layer, suggesting a hierarchical encoding mechanism.
Transformer-based models (BERT) are more sensitive to context length overall, and their first layer is more context-dependent than the last layer.
Among the models, UniSentEnc learns very different representations from the others, possibly due to different training objectives.
LSTM-based models achieve higher similarity with brain data compared to GloVe and transformer-based models, and their lower layers align better with brain representations.
papers.limitation:
Standard RSA assumes all features of the representational spaces have equal contributions, leading to information loss.
The representational similarity between all models and the brain images remains very low.
Inherent issues in the brain data (e.g., hemodynamic response delay, noise) and complexity of the story reading task make evaluation hard.
future_direction: Perform further analysis on various (bigger) datasets to better interpret what is happening in both the brain and computational models.
Postpone further analysis with the predictive approach (linear regression) to future studies.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we define and apply representational stability analysis (ReStA), an intuitive way of analyzing neural language models. ReStA is a variant of the popular representational similarity analysis (RSA) in cognitive neuroscience. While RSA can be used to compare representations in models, model components, and human brains, ReStA compares instances of the same model, while systematically varying single model parameter. Using ReStA, we study four recent and successful neural language models, and evaluate how sensitive their internal representations are to the amount of prior context. Using RSA, we perform a systematic study of how similar the representational spaces in the first and second (or higher) layers of these models are to each other and to patterns of activation in the human brain. Our results reveal surprisingly strong differences between language models, and give insights into where the deep linguistic processing, that integrates information over multiple sentences, is happening in these models. The combination of ReStA and RSA on models and brains allows us to start addressing the important question of what kind of linguistic processes we can hope to observe in fMRI brain imaging data. In particular, our results suggest that the data on story reading from Wehbe et al. (2014) contains a signal of shallow linguistic processing, but show no evidence on the more interesting deep linguistic processing.

papers.title: Intrinsic Robotic Introspection: Learning Internal States From Neuron Activations
papers.research_question: How to extract abstract representations of internal states from artificial neural networks and how these representations can be used to inform the execution of a robotic manipulation task.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an introspective framework that uses a Variational Autoencoder to learn internal states from neural network activations, demonstrating that these states improve the training convergence and success rate of a behavior-based reinforcement learning agent in a robotic manipulation task.
papers.conclusion: Internal states improve the performance of BBRL by incorporating environment observation and hidden activations, enabling faster learning of the robotic task, as supported by statistical significance analysis.
papers.key_findings:
Using internal states as input to the actor-critic reduces the number of training episodes needed for convergence by about 1300 episodes.
Concatenating latent means and log variances as input results in the fastest convergence and highest success value.
Internal states improve the state values for all robotic behaviors (approach, grasp, retract).
The approach is robust to noise in the input, maintaining performance with 5% and 10% noise levels.
The latent space learned by the VAE encodes temporal transitions between behaviors, as visualized with t-SNE.
future_direction: Explore using internal states to dictate the behavior of BBRL instead of using an actor-critic.
Adopt an unsupervised learning approach to train the robot.
Explore how internal states can be evolved using evolutionary techniques to improve performance and acquire new skills.
papers.abstract: We present an introspective framework inspired by the process of how humans perform introspection. Our working assumption is that neural network activations encode information, and building internal states from these activations can improve the performance of an actor-critic model. We perform experiments where we first train a Variational Autoencoder model to reconstruct the activations of a feature extraction network and use the latent space to improve the performance of an actor-critic when deciding which low-level robotic behaviour to execute. We show that internal states reduce the number of episodes needed by about 1300 episodes while training an actor-critic, denoting faster convergence to get a high success value while completing a robotic task.

papers.title: Influential Training Data Retrieval for Explaining Verbalized Confidence of LLMs
papers.research_question: What drives confidence in LLMs, and do they ground their confidence in content-related training examples or superficial confidence-related cues?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces TracVC, a method for tracing verbalized confidence in LLMs back to training data, and finds that LLMs often rely on superficial confidence cues rather than content grounding.
papers.conclusion: TracVC reveals that LLMs are often influenced by confidence-related training data, indicating a limitation in current training regimes. The method provides a data-centric approach for improving trustworthiness in confidence expression.
papers.key_findings:
OLMo2-13B is frequently influenced by confidence-related training data that is lexically unrelated to the query, suggesting it mimics linguistic expressions of certainty.
Larger LLMs do not demonstrate higher content groundness than smaller ones, possibly due to higher sensitivity to stylistic patterns.
Content groundness is higher when tested on samples that are correctly answered by the LLM.
Post-training techniques can impact content groundness in opposite directions on different LLMs.
LLMs may learn to sound confident without understanding when confidence is justified, highlighting a limitation in training regimes.
papers.limitation:
Constrained to a limited set of LLMs, primarily OLMo and Llama families, due to data availability.
Simplified separation of content- and confidence-related influences, which may overlap in practice.
Limited coverage due to retrieval-based approach and fixed number of retrieved examples.
Use of TracIn for influence estimation, without comparison to alternative methods like Hessian-based approaches.
future_direction: Future research on how pre-training and fine-tuning strategies shape confidence grounding.
Extending TracVC to study other aspects of model behavior like answer selection and reasoning patterns.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can increase users' perceived trust by verbalizing confidence in their outputs. However, prior work has shown that LLMs are often overconfident, making their stated confidence unreliable since it does not consistently align with factual accuracy. To better understand the sources of this verbalized confidence, we introduce TracVC (\textbf{Trac}ing \textbf{V}erbalized \textbf{C}onfidence), a method that builds on information retrieval and influence estimation to trace generated confidence expressions back to the training data. We evaluate TracVC on OLMo and Llama models in a question answering setting, proposing a new metric, content groundness, which measures the extent to which an LLM grounds its confidence in content-related training examples (relevant to the question and answer) versus in generic examples of confidence verbalization. Our analysis reveals that OLMo2-13B is frequently influenced by confidence-related data that is lexically unrelated to the query, suggesting that it may mimic superficial linguistic expressions of certainty rather than rely on genuine content grounding. These findings point to a fundamental limitation in current training regimes: LLMs may learn how to sound confident without learning when confidence is justified. Our analysis provides a foundation for improving LLMs' trustworthiness in expressing more reliable confidence.

papers.title: Unraveling Token Prediction Refinement and Identifying Essential Layers in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models iteratively refine token predictions through internal processing, and how does the positioning of relevant information within the input context affect this refinement process?
papers.core_contribution: The study finds that the depth of token prediction refinement in LLMs, measured by the number of layers between the first correct prediction and its finalization, follows an inverted U-shaped curve relative to the position of relevant information in the input context, with more refinement needed when information is in the middle of long contexts.
papers.conclusion: Investigating intermediate representations using the logit lens provides insights into how LLMs iteratively refine token predictions, which is vital for advancing AI safety research and developing secure, human-aligned AI technologies.
papers.key_findings:
The depth of prediction refinement (layers between initial correct token and final stable output) varies with the position of relevant information, showing an approximately inverted U-shaped curve.
The gap between the layer where the top-1 token first matches the correct answer and where it is finalized is smaller when relevant information is at the beginning or end of the input context.
Not all layers are equally essential for determining final correct outputs; the positioning of relevant information impacts which layers are critical.
The logit lens reveals that early layers produce plausible but inaccurate token predictions, which are gradually refined in middle and later layers.
The model's ability to capture dependency relations and compositional understanding is observed, but may struggle with longer contexts where relevant information is positioned in the middle.
papers.limitation:
The effectiveness of the logit lens varies significantly depending on the task and model used; for tasks requiring deep, abstract reasoning, layers far from the output may offer little relevant information when analyzed solely through token prediction.
Reducing complex layer representations to token predictions introduces biases, as many layers may serve other functions (e.g., refining internal features or re-weighting contextual information) not captured by logits.
Token distributions can be highly skewed, with some tokens dominating, which may obscure the true purpose or significance of intermediate representations.
The logit lens alone does not fully reveal the layered, nuanced, and abstract processes underlying a language model's true capabilities and must be combined with other techniques for a comprehensive understanding.
papers.abstract: This research aims to unravel how large language models (LLMs) iteratively refine token predictions through internal processing. We utilized a logit lens technique to analyze the model's token predictions derived from intermediate representations. Specifically, we focused on (1) how LLMs access and utilize information from input contexts, and (2) how positioning of relevant information affects the model's token prediction refinement process. On a multi-document question answering task with varying input context lengths, we found that the depth of prediction refinement (defined as the number of intermediate layers an LLM uses to transition from an initial correct token prediction to its final, stable correct output), as a function of the position of relevant information, exhibits an approximately inverted U-shaped curve. We also found that the gap between these two layers, on average, diminishes when relevant information is positioned at the beginning or end of the input context. This suggested that the model requires more refinements when processing longer contexts with relevant information situated in the middle. Furthermore, our findings indicate that not all layers are equally essential for determining final correct outputs. Our analysis provides insights into how token predictions are distributed across different conditions, and establishes important connections to existing hypotheses and previous findings in AI safety research and development.

papers.title: Does Representation Matter? Exploring Intermediate Layers in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What defines a 'good' representation in large language models, and how does the quality of intermediate representations compare to final layers across different architectures and settings?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that intermediate layers of LLMs often provide better representations for downstream tasks than final layers, and reveals significant differences in representation quality and evolution between Transformer and State Space Model (SSM) architectures.
papers.conclusion: The research advances understanding of internal representation dynamics in LLMs, highlighting the pivotal role of intermediate layers and the distinct behaviors of Transformer and SSM architectures, providing guidance for model optimization.
papers.key_findings:
Intermediate layers consistently outperform final layers on downstream embedding tasks from the MTEB benchmark.
Prompt entropy in intermediate layers is negatively correlated with MMLU performance for Transformers like Llama3, but not for SSMs like Mamba2.
Transformers exhibit greater representational variability and information compression in intermediate layers, while SSMs show more stable representations across layers.
Training effects on representation quality are most pronounced in intermediate layers, with prompt entropy decreasing and InfoNCE peaking as training progresses.
Extreme input conditions (token repetition, randomness, and length) distinctly affect prompt entropy, particularly in intermediate layers, and a bimodal entropy distribution is observed in Transformer intermediate layers with an unknown cause.
papers.limitation: The cause of the bimodal entropy distribution observed in intermediate layers of Transformer models remains unknown.
future_direction: Investigate the causes of bimodal entropy distributions in intermediate layers.
Explore the development of new metrics specifically tailored to LLMs for representation evaluation.
papers.abstract: Understanding what defines a good representation in large language models (LLMs) is fundamental to both theoretical understanding and practical applications. In this paper, we investigate the quality of intermediate representations in various LLM architectures, including Transformers and State Space Models (SSMs). We find that intermediate layers often yield more informative representations for downstream tasks than the final layers. To measure the representation quality, we adapt and apply a suite of metrics - such as prompt entropy, curvature, and augmentation-invariance - originally proposed in other contexts. Our empirical study reveals significant architectural differences, how representations evolve throughout training, and how factors like input randomness and prompt length affect each layer. Notably, we observe a bimodal pattern in the entropy of some intermediate layers and consider potential explanations tied to training data. Overall, our results illuminate the internal mechanics of LLMs and guide strategies for architectural optimization and training.

papers.title: On Epistemic Uncertainty of Visual Tokens for Object Hallucinations in Large Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: How does the epistemic uncertainty of visual tokens from the vision encoder contribute to object hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs), and can mitigating this uncertainty reduce hallucinations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that visual tokens with high epistemic uncertainty are a key factor in object hallucination in LVLMs, and proposes a training-free method to mitigate hallucinations by identifying these uncertain tokens via adversarial perturbations and masking them in the self-attention layers of the vision encoder.
papers.conclusion: Uncertain visual tokens from the vision encoder are a key contributor to object hallucination in LVLMs, and the proposed training-free masking method effectively mitigates hallucinations by suppressing these tokens, offering a complementary approach to existing methods.
papers.key_findings:
Visual tokens with high epistemic uncertainty, as estimated by representation deviation under adversarial perturbations, are strongly positively correlated with object hallucination in LVLMs.
The norm of representation deviation under small adversarial perturbations efficiently approximates an upper bound of epistemic uncertainty for visual tokens, particularly in early vision encoder layers.
Masking uncertain visual tokens in the self-attention process of intermediate vision encoder layers significantly reduces object hallucination across multiple LVLM architectures and benchmarks.
The proposed method is orthogonal and compatible with existing language-model-focused hallucination mitigation techniques, enabling synergistic performance gains.
The method reduces the average uncertainty of visual tokens, and this reduction correlates with improved hallucination metrics.
papers.limitation:
The method requires additional computational overhead for generating adversarial perturbations to identify uncertain tokens.
The threshold parameter for binarizing the uncertainty mask needs to be tuned for different models and decoding strategies.
The method may not address all types of hallucinations, such as those arising from the language model itself or from complex reasoning errors.
future_direction: Extending the uncertainty estimation and masking approach to other modalities and tasks beyond object hallucination.
Improving the efficiency of the uncertainty estimation process to reduce computational overhead.
Exploring the integration of the proposed vision-encoder-focused method with more advanced language-model-based mitigation techniques.
papers.abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs), which integrate a vision encoder (VE) with a large language model, have achieved remarkable success across various tasks. However, there are still crucial challenges in LVLMs such as object hallucination, generating descriptions of objects that are not in the input image. Here, we argue that uncertain visual tokens within the VE is a key factor that contributes to object hallucination. Our statistical analysis found that there are positive correlations between visual tokens with high epistemic uncertainty and the occurrence of hallucinations. Furthermore, we show theoretically and empirically that visual tokens in early VE layers that exhibit large representation deviations under small adversarial perturbations indicate high epistemic uncertainty. Based on these findings, we propose a simple yet effective strategy to mitigate object hallucination by modifying the VE only. Our method comprises a proxy method with adversarial perturbations for identifying uncertain visual tokens efficiently and a method to mask these uncertain visual tokens during the self-attention process in the middle layers of the VE, suppressing their influence on visual encoding and thus alleviating hallucinations. Extensive experiments show that our method significantly reduces object hallucinations in LVLMs and can synergistically work with other prior arts.

papers.title: Retrieval Head Mechanistically Explains Long-Context Factuality
papers.research_question: How do long-context language models retrieve relevant information from arbitrary locations within the input?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers and characterizes 'retrieval heads', a sparse set of attention heads responsible for retrieving information from long contexts, and shows they are universal, intrinsic, and causally important for factuality and reasoning.
papers.conclusion: Retrieval heads implement a conditional copy algorithm and are the primary reason why long-context models can pass the Needle-in-a-Haystack test; their activation explains model factuality versus hallucination.
papers.key_findings:
Retrieval heads are universal and sparse, existing in all tested long-context models and constituting less than 5% of attention heads.
Retrieval heads are intrinsic, already present in base models and reused in derived models (e.g., via continued pretraining or fine-tuning).
Retrieval heads are dynamically activated based on the specific tokens and context required for retrieval.
Retrieval heads are causal; pruning them leads to retrieval failure and hallucination, while pruning non-retrieval heads does not.
Retrieval heads strongly influence chain-of-thought reasoning tasks, which require frequent reference to input information, but have less impact on tasks relying on internal knowledge.
future_direction: Fostering future research on reducing hallucination, improving reasoning, and compressing the KV cache.
Discovering more algorithm and functionalities implemented by other types of attention heads.
Applying insights to KV cache compression by pruning non-retrieval head caches.
papers.abstract: Despite the recent progress in long-context language models, it remains elusive how transformer-based models exhibit the capability to retrieve relevant information from arbitrary locations within the long context. This paper aims to address this question. Our systematic investigation across a wide spectrum of models reveals that a special type of attention heads are largely responsible for retrieving information, which we dub retrieval heads. We identify intriguing properties of retrieval heads:(1) universal: all the explored models with long-context capability have a set of retrieval heads; (2) sparse: only a small portion (less than 5\%) of the attention heads are retrieval. (3) intrinsic: retrieval heads already exist in models pretrained with short context. When extending the context length by continual pretraining, it is still the same set of heads that perform information retrieval. (4) dynamically activated: take Llama-2 7B for example, 12 retrieval heads always attend to the required information no matter how the context is changed. The rest of the retrieval heads are activated in different contexts. (5) causal: completely pruning retrieval heads leads to failure in retrieving relevant information and results in hallucination, while pruning random non-retrieval heads does not affect the model's retrieval ability. We further show that retrieval heads strongly influence chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning, where the model needs to frequently refer back the question and previously-generated context. Conversely, tasks where the model directly generates the answer using its intrinsic knowledge are less impacted by masking out retrieval heads. These observations collectively explain which internal part of the model seeks information from the input tokens. We believe our insights will foster future research on reducing hallucination, improving reasoning, and compressing the KV cache.

papers.title: Large Language Models Are Cross-Lingual Knowledge-Free Reasoners
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between cross-lingual transferability and the components of reasoning tasks (knowledge retrieval vs. knowledge-free reasoning)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that knowledge-free reasoning capability transfers nearly perfectly across languages, whereas knowledge retrieval significantly hinders cross-lingual transfer, attributed to shared neural mechanisms for reasoning and language-specific knowledge storage.
papers.conclusion: The demand for knowledge retrieval significantly hinders cross-lingual transfer performance, while knowledge-free reasoning ability can be nearly fully transferred between languages, due to shared neural mechanisms for reasoning and language-specific knowledge storage.
papers.key_findings:
The knowledge retrieval component significantly hinders cross-lingual transfer in reasoning tasks; more knowledge retrieval leads to lower transfer effectiveness.
Knowledge-free reasoning capability can be nearly perfectly transferred across languages after fine-tuning in one language.
Cross-lingual computational similarity (hidden states and neuron activation) is higher for knowledge-free reasoning than for knowledge retrieval, especially in middle layers.
Target language proficiency impacts transferability; improving proficiency enhances cross-lingual transfer for knowledge-free reasoning.
The model uses similar neurons for knowledge-free reasoning across languages, while knowledge is stored separately in different languages.
papers.limitation:
Limited model selection and language coverage, primarily relying on LLaMA-2 and only ten languages.
Depth of interpretability analysis is limited; macro-level numerical analyses without precisely identifying specific neurons.
future_direction: Conduct more detailed neuron-level analyses to verify hypotheses about shared neurons for reasoning and language-specific knowledge storage.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models have demonstrated impressive reasoning capabilities across multiple languages. However, the relationship between capabilities in different languages is less explored. In this work, we decompose the process of reasoning tasks into two separated components: knowledge retrieval and knowledge-free reasoning, and analyze the relationship between cross-lingual transferability and these two components. With adapted commonsense reasoning datasets and constructed knowledge-free reasoning datasets, we show that the knowledge-free reasoning capability can be nearly perfectly transferred across various source-target language directions despite the secondary impact of resource in some specific target languages, while cross-lingual knowledge retrieval significantly hinders the transfer. Moreover, by analyzing the hidden states and feed-forward network neuron activation during the reasoning, we show that higher similarity of hidden representations and larger overlap of activated neurons could explain the better cross-lingual transferability of knowledge-free reasoning than knowledge retrieval. Thus, we hypothesize that knowledge-free reasoning shares similar neurons in different languages for reasoning, while knowledge is stored separately in different languages. Our code and data is available at: https://github.com/NJUNLP/Knowledge-Free-Reasoning.

papers.title: Exploring Activation Patterns of Parameters in Language Models
papers.research_question: Which parameters within the network are activated to determine the outputs, and does the distribution of these activated weights exhibit distinct patterns when faced with inputs across different domains?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a gradient-based metric to assess parameter activation in LLMs and finds that shallow layers activate densely for same-domain inputs while deep layers activate sparsely, shallow layers show higher activation similarity across domains than deep layers, and deep layer activation similarity correlates with data relevance.
papers.conclusion: The paper explores activation patterns in LLMs using a gradient-based metric and LLMDcos, finding distinct layer-wise patterns and validating them through experiments.
papers.key_findings:
For inputs in the same domain, parameters in shallow layers are activated densely, while parameters in deep layers are activated sparsely.
For inputs across different domains, parameters in shallow layers exhibit higher similarity in activation behavior than in deep layers.
In deep layers, the similarity of the distributions of activated parameters is positively correlated to the empirical data relevance.
papers.limitation:
GPU memory limitations prevent verification of pruning results on larger models like Llama2-70B.
The activation degree algorithm is a very rough calculation; more refined calculations are constrained by time and space complexities.
papers.abstract: Most work treats large language models as black boxes without an in-depth understanding of their internal working mechanism. To explain the internal representations of LLMs, we utilize a gradient-based metric to assess the activation level of model parameters. Based on this metric, we obtain three preliminary findings. (1) When the inputs are in the same domain, parameters in the shallow layers will be activated densely, which means a larger portion of parameters will have great impacts on the outputs. In contrast, parameters in the deep layers are activated sparsely. (2) When the inputs are across different domains, parameters in shallow layers exhibit higher similarity in the activation behavior than in deep layers. (3) In deep layers, the similarity of the distributions of activated parameters is positively correlated to the empirical data relevance. Further, we develop three validation experiments to solidify these findings. (1) Firstly, starting from the first finding, we attempt to configure different sparsities for different layers and find this method can benefit model pruning. (2) Secondly, we find that a pruned model based on one calibration set can better handle tasks related to the calibration task than those not related, which validates the second finding. (3) Thirdly, Based on the STS-B and SICK benchmarks, we find that two sentences with consistent semantics tend to share similar parameter activation patterns in deep layers, which aligns with our third finding. Our work sheds light on the behavior of parameter activation in LLMs, and we hope these findings will have the potential to inspire more practical applications.

papers.title: Large Language Models Are Human-Like Internally
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether surprisal (negative log probability) from internal layers of large language models aligns with human sentence processing data, and whether the alignment varies by layer depth and the type of human measure (behavioral vs. neurophysiological).
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that surprisal from internal layers of larger language models aligns well with human sentence processing data, challenging prior conclusions that focused on final layers. Additionally, it finds that earlier layers align with fast human measures (e.g., gaze duration) and later layers with slower measures (e.g., N400).
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that larger language models are cognitively plausible when internal layers are considered, and that different layers correspond to different stages of human sentence processing, advocating for layer-wise alignment in cognitive modeling.
papers.key_findings:
Surprisal from internal layers of larger LMs aligns with human sentence processing data as well as or better than smaller LMs.
The last layer does not yield the best alignment; the best layer varies by human measure.
Earlier layers align better with fast human measures (e.g., first-pass gaze duration, self-paced reading time), while later layers align better with slower measures (e.g., N400, MAZE processing time).
When considering the best internal layer, larger LMs show a positive scaling effect (larger models have higher ∆LL) for most human measures.
The alignment patterns are consistent across multiple languages (tested on MECO corpus).
papers.limitation: The study is focused on naturalistic reading corpora and does not include controlled experiments on syntactic ambiguity or grammatical violation, which are known challenges for surprisal theory.
