future_direction: Extend the analysis to other probability-based measures such as entropy and entropy reduction.
Combine the internal layer approach with linguistically-motivated neural models.
papers.abstract: Recent cognitive modeling studies have reported that larger language models (LMs) exhibit a poorer fit to human reading behavior (Oh and Schuler, 2023b; Shain et al., 2024; Kuribayashi et al., 2024), leading to claims of their cognitive implausibility. In this paper, we revisit this argument through the lens of mechanistic interpretability and argue that prior conclusions were skewed by an exclusive focus on the final layers of LMs. Our analysis reveals that next-word probabilities derived from internal layers of larger LMs align with human sentence processing data as well as, or better than, those from smaller LMs. This alignment holds consistently across behavioral (self-paced reading times, gaze durations, MAZE task processing times) and neurophysiological (N400 brain potentials) measures, challenging earlier mixed results and suggesting that the cognitive plausibility of larger LMs has been underestimated. Furthermore, we first identify an intriguing relationship between LM layers and human measures: earlier layers correspond more closely with fast gaze durations, while later layers better align with relatively slower signals such as N400 potentials and MAZE processing times. Our work opens new avenues for interdisciplinary research at the intersection of mechanistic interpretability and cognitive modeling.

papers.title: Steering Llama 2 via Contrastive Activation Addition
papers.research_question: How can we steer language models by adding contrastive activation vectors to the residual stream, and how effective is this method?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA), a method for steering language models by adding contrastive activation vectors to the residual stream, which effectively steers behavior, works on top of finetuning and system prompts, and minimally reduces capabilities.
papers.conclusion: CAA is an effective method for steering LLMs, providing precise control over behavior with minimal performance degradation, and offers insights into the linear representations of abstract concepts in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
CAA can effectively steer Llama 2 Chat models on a variety of alignment-relevant behaviors (AI Coordination, Corrigibility, Hallucination, Myopic Reward, Survival Instinct, Sycophancy, Refusal).
CAA generalizes from multiple-choice to open-ended generation tasks.
CAA can be combined with system prompting and finetuning to further control behavior.
CAA has minimal impact on general capabilities as measured by MMLU.
The steering vectors correspond intuitively to the presence of the behavior in the generated tokens (as shown by cosine similarity).
papers.limitation:
GPT-4 evaluation has limitations (sensitivity to prompt wording, biases).
Finetuning baseline was not fully optimized (hyperparameters, loss function).
Prompting baseline may not be fully optimized.
Vector normalization choices (norms vary across layers and behaviors).
future_direction: Steering at targeted token positions (instead of all tokens after the prompt).
Steering outside the residual stream (e.g., after MLP).
Application to red-teaming (using CAA to trigger unwanted behaviors).
papers.abstract: Nina Rimsky, Nick Gabrieli, Julian Schulz, Meg Tong, Evan Hubinger, Alexander Turner. Proceedings of the 62nd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2024.

papers.title: Start Making Sense(s): A Developmental Probe of Attention Specialization Using Lexical Ambiguity
papers.research_question: How do attention heads in Transformer language models develop specialized attention patterns for word sense disambiguation, and how robust are these heads to stimulus perturbations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a developmental pipeline to probe attention specialization in Transformer LMs, using lexical ambiguity to identify and causally validate attention heads involved in word sense disambiguation, finding that larger models have more robust disambiguation heads.
papers.conclusion: Disambiguation benefits from a constellation of mechanisms, some of which are highly sensitive to cue position and part-of-speech (especially in smaller models), while larger models contain more robust disambiguation heads, highlighting the value of a developmental perspective in probing LM mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Disambiguation performance improves with model size but with diminishing returns, with 410M achieving 92% of the performance of 12B despite having 3% as many parameters.
Inflection points in disambiguation performance occur early in pre-training (e.g., at steps 1000 and 2000).
In Pythia-14M, specific attention heads (e.g., (3,1) and (3,2)) show attention patterns that covary with disambiguation performance.
In Pythia-410M, multiple heads across layers show robust disambiguation behavior, generalizing across stimulus perturbations like positional and part-of-speech changes.
Ablating identified heads causally impairs disambiguation performance, especially in Pythia-14M, confirming their functional role.
papers.abstract: Despite an in-principle understanding of self-attention matrix operations in Transformer language models (LMs), it remains unclear precisely how these operations map onto interpretable computations or functions--and how or when individual attention heads develop specialized attention patterns. Here, we present a pipeline to systematically probe attention mechanisms, and we illustrate its value by leveraging lexical ambiguity--where a single word has multiple meanings--to isolate attention mechanisms that contribute to word sense disambiguation. We take a "developmental" approach: first, using publicly available Pythia LM checkpoints, we identify inflection points in disambiguation performance for each LM in the suite; in 14M and 410M, we identify heads whose attention to disambiguating words covaries with overall disambiguation performance across development. We then stress-test the robustness of these heads to stimulus perturbations: in 14M, we find limited robustness, but in 410M, we identify multiple heads with surprisingly generalizable behavior. Then, in a causal analysis, we find that ablating the target heads demonstrably impairs disambiguation performance, particularly in 14M. We additionally reproduce developmental analyses of 14M across all of its random seeds. Together, these results suggest: that disambiguation benefits from a constellation of mechanisms, some of which (especially in 14M) are highly sensitive to the position and part-of-speech of the disambiguating cue; and that larger models (410M) may contain heads with more robust disambiguation behavior. They also join a growing body of work that highlights the value of adopting a developmental perspective when probing LM mechanisms.

papers.title: Distilled Circuits: A Mechanistic Study of Internal Restructuring in Knowledge Distillation
papers.research_question: How does knowledge distillation restructure internal circuits and representations in student models, and how can functional alignment between teacher and student be quantified?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a mechanistic understanding of how knowledge distillation restructures internal circuits, showing that students compress and discard teacher components, and introduces an alignment metric to quantify functional alignment beyond output similarity.
papers.conclusion: While student models preserve broad functional behavior from their teachers, knowledge distillation causes significant internal circuit restructuring, leading to increased reliance on fewer components and reduced robustness. The alignment metric captures functional similarity beyond output behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Student models reorganize, compress, and discard teacher components, leading to stronger reliance on fewer components.
Student models are more vulnerable to component ablation, indicating reduced robustness.
The introduced alignment metric effectively quantifies functional alignment between teacher and student models.
These findings on internal restructuring and reduced robustness generalize across different model architectures (GPT2, BERT, Llama).
Performance similarity does not guarantee similarity in internal computation; circuit-level analysis is essential for understanding functional alignment.
papers.limitation:
The study is constrained by the relatively small set of models evaluated (6).
The component role attribution procedure is manual and could be automated.
The alignment metric could be improved in granularity and interpretability.
The findings are based on specific tasks and models and may not generalize to all settings.
future_direction: Apply the methodology and alignment metric to a broader, more diverse collection of models.
Automate the component role attribution procedure, potentially using interpretability agents.
Improve the alignment metric's granularity and interpretability, and explore incorporating it as a loss term during distillation.
papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses a larger neural model (teacher) into smaller, faster student models by training them to match teacher outputs. However, the internal computational transformations that occur during this process remain poorly understood. We apply techniques from mechanistic interpretability to analyze how internal circuits, representations, and activation patterns differ between teacher and student. Focusing on GPT2-small and its distilled counterpart DistilGPT2, we find that student models reorganize, compress, and discard teacher components, often resulting in stronger reliance on fewer individual components. To quantify functional alignment beyond output similarity, we introduce an alignment metric based on influence-weighted component similarity, validated across multiple tasks. Our findings reveal that while knowledge distillation preserves broad functional behaviors, it also causes significant shifts in internal computation, with important implications for the robustness and generalization capacity of distilled models.

papers.title: Understanding Transformer Memorization Recall Through Idioms
papers.research_question: When does a model decide to output a memorized phrase, and how is this phrase then retrieved from memory?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a methodological framework and dataset for probing memorization recall in transformers, and finds that memorized predictions involve a two-step process of candidate promotion in early layers and confidence boosting in upper layers.
papers.conclusion: Overall, our work makes a first step towards understanding memory recall, and provides a methodological basis for future studies of transformer memorization.
papers.key_findings:
Memorized predictions are a two-step process: early layers promote the predicted token to the top of the output distribution, and upper layers increase model confidence.
Memorized information is stored and retrieved in the early layers of the network.
The first layer is especially critical for memorized predictions.
The findings generalize from idioms to factual statements.
The IDIO MEM dataset is constructed for probing memorization and released for the community.
papers.abstract: To produce accurate predictions, language models (LMs) must balance between generalization and memorization. Yet, little is known about the mechanism by which transformer LMs employ their memorization capacity. When does a model decide to output a memorized phrase, and how is this phrase then retrieved from memory? In this work, we offer the first methodological framework for probing and characterizing recall of memorized sequences in transformer LMs. First, we lay out criteria for detecting model inputs that trigger memory recall, and propose idioms as inputs that typically fulfill these criteria. Next, we construct a dataset of English idioms and use it to compare model behavior on memorized vs. non-memorized inputs. Specifically, we analyze the internal prediction construction process by interpreting the model's hidden representations as a gradual refinement of the output probability distribution. We find that across different model sizes and architectures, memorized predictions are a two-step process: early layers promote the predicted token to the top of the output distribution, and upper layers increase model confidence. This suggests that memorized information is stored and retrieved in the early layers of the network. Last, we demonstrate the utility of our methodology beyond idioms in memorized factual statements. Overall, our work makes a first step towards understanding memory recall, and provides a methodological basis for future studies of transformer memorization.

papers.title: ShortGPT: Layers in Large Language Models are More Redundant Than You Expect
papers.research_question: How redundant are the layers in large language models, and can a simple layer removal method based on a new importance metric effectively prune them?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies significant layer redundancy in LLMs and introduces Block Influence (BI) to measure layer importance. Based on BI, the proposed ShortGPT method removes redundant layers, achieving competitive pruning results without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit significant layer-wise redundancy, and a simple pruning method based on layer removal (ShortGPT) can effectively compress models with minimal performance loss, offering insights for future model compression and training efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Layers in LLMs are redundant, especially in the middle to later layers, and removing them individually causes minimal performance degradation.
The proposed Block Influence (BI) metric, based on cosine similarity between a layer's input and output hidden states, correlates with layer importance.
ShortGPT, a simple layer removal method based on BI, outperforms previous state-of-the-art pruning methods and maintains ~90% performance while reducing ~25% parameters.
The redundancy phenomenon is not unique to transformers; it also exists in non-transformer models like Mamba and RWKV.
ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization and can be combined with it for further compression.
papers.limitation: Layer removal has a more significant negative effect on generative tasks compared to multiple-choice tasks, especially for smaller models.
future_direction: Exploring post-training to restore performance after pruning
Improving model training efficiency by reducing inherent redundancy
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to advance in performance, their size has escalated significantly, with current LLMs containing billions or even trillions of parameters. However, in this study, we discovered that many layers of LLMs exhibit high similarity, and some layers play a negligible role in network functionality. Based on this observation, we define a metric called Block Influence (BI) to gauge the significance of each layer in LLMs. We then propose a straightforward pruning approach: layer removal, in which we directly delete the redundant layers in LLMs based on their BI scores. Experiments demonstrate that our method, which we call ShortGPT, significantly outperforms previous state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods in model pruning. Moreover, ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization-like methods, enabling further reduction in parameters and computation. The ability to achieve better results through simple layer removal, as opposed to more complex pruning techniques, suggests a high degree of redundancy in the model architecture.

papers.title: Reasoning as State Transition: A Representational Analysis of Reasoning Evolution in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How does reasoning ability evolve during training in large language models, and what is the role of internal representation dynamics in this process?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a representational analysis framework showing that post-training yields limited improvement in static initial representation quality, but reasoning involves a continuous distributional shift in representations during generation, which post-training enhances to drive representations toward a better state for task solving.
papers.conclusion: The work provides a novel representational perspective on reasoning evolution in LLMs, highlighting the importance of internal state dynamics and the role of post-training in enhancing state transitions, offering insights for future model analysis and optimization.
papers.key_findings:
Post-training yields only limited improvement in static initial representation quality.
Reasoning involves a significant continuous distributional shift in representations during generation, unlike non-reasoning tasks.
Post-training empowers models to drive this representation transition toward a better distribution for task solving.
There is a high correlation between generation correctness and final representations, but low correlation with initial representations.
The semantic content of the generated tokens is the dominant driver of the state transition, not additional computation or intrinsic parameter differences.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models have achieved remarkable performance on reasoning tasks, motivating research into how this ability evolves during training. Prior work has primarily analyzed this evolution via explicit generation outcomes, treating the reasoning process as a black box and obscuring internal changes. To address this opacity, we introduce a representational perspective to investigate the dynamics of the model's internal states. Through comprehensive experiments across models at various training stages, we discover that post-training yields only limited improvement in static initial representation quality. Furthermore, we reveal that, distinct from non-reasoning tasks, reasoning involves a significant continuous distributional shift in representations during generation. Comparative analysis indicates that post-training empowers models to drive this transition toward a better distribution for task solving. To clarify the relationship between internal states and external outputs, statistical analysis confirms a high correlation between generation correctness and the final representations; while counterfactual experiments identify the semantics of the generated tokens, rather than additional computation during inference or intrinsic parameter differences, as the dominant driver of the transition. Collectively, we offer a novel understanding of the reasoning process and the effect of training on reasoning enhancement, providing valuable insights for future model analysis and optimization.

papers.title: Learning Inductive Biases with Simple Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How do simple neural networks develop inductive biases like the shape bias, and under what conditions? How does the acquisition of this bias relate to vocabulary acceleration, mirroring child development?
papers.core_contribution: Simple neural networks can learn a shape bias from very few examples, and the development of this bias predicts vocabulary acceleration in the networks, consistent with developmental processes in children.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks can learn inductive biases like the shape bias from limited data, and the dynamics of this learning mirror child development, suggesting a connection between artificial and human learning.
papers.key_findings:
Multilayer perceptrons develop a shape bias after seeing as few as 3 examples of 4 object categories using abstract bit-vector patterns.
Convolutional neural networks develop a shape bias with as few as 6 examples of 8 object categories using synthetic images.
Networks show greater sensitivity to changes in shape than color after shape bias training, as shown by parametric manipulation of stimuli.
The development of the shape bias in CNNs correlates with the onset of vocabulary acceleration, mirroring the correlation observed in children.
Color bias training requires less data than shape bias training and does not follow the same two-step generalization process.
future_direction: Investigate the hypothesis of initializing large-scale image recognition models with shape bias training using ImageNet-scale DNNs.
papers.abstract: People use rich prior knowledge about the world in order to efficiently learn new concepts. These priors - also known as "inductive biases" - pertain to the space of internal models considered by a learner, and they help the learner make inferences that go beyond the observed data. A recent study found that deep neural networks optimized for object recognition develop the shape bias (Ritter et al., 2017), an inductive bias possessed by children that plays an important role in early word learning. However, these networks use unrealistically large quantities of training data, and the conditions required for these biases to develop are not well understood. Moreover, it is unclear how the learning dynamics of these networks relate to developmental processes in childhood. We investigate the development and influence of the shape bias in neural networks using controlled datasets of abstract patterns and synthetic images, allowing us to systematically vary the quantity and form of the experience provided to the learning algorithms. We find that simple neural networks develop a shape bias after seeing as few as 3 examples of 4 object categories. The development of these biases predicts the onset of vocabulary acceleration in our networks, consistent with the developmental process in children.

papers.title: Summing Up the Facts: Additive Mechanisms Behind Factual Recall in LLMs
papers.research_question: How do transformer-based large language models (LLMs) store and retrieve factual knowledge? The paper investigates the mechanistic story behind factual recall, focusing on prompts of the form 'Fact: The Colosseum is in the country of ____.'
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that factual recall in LLMs is achieved through an additive combination of multiple independent mechanisms (subject heads, relation heads, mixed heads, MLPs), termed the 'additive motif', and extends direct logit attribution to attribute attention head outputs to individual source tokens.
papers.conclusion: Factual recall in LLMs is achieved through additive combination of multiple independent mechanisms, and this additive motif may be a general principle in how models compute.
papers.key_findings:
There are four distinct mechanisms (subject heads, relation heads, mixed heads, MLPs) that additively combine to produce factual recall.
Each mechanism independently contributes to the correct logit, and their sum results in constructive interference, even if individual mechanisms are insufficient alone.
The additive motif explains why models often produce incorrect attributes alongside correct ones.
Extending direct logit attribution to attribute head outputs to source tokens reveals mixed heads as two separate additive updates from subject and relation tokens.
The work highlights a limitation of narrow circuit analysis that ignores multiple sources of information in prompts.
papers.limitation:
The dataset is small and hand-written, which may limit generalizability.
The analysis is limited to a specific prompting format and may not generalize to other tasks.
future_direction: Understanding correlation and superposition in feature representations
Understanding MLP neurons in detail
Studying how different prompting setups affect factual recall mechanisms
papers.abstract: How do transformer-based large language models (LLMs) store and retrieve knowledge? We focus on the most basic form of this task -- factual recall, where the model is tasked with explicitly surfacing stored facts in prompts of form `Fact: The Colosseum is in the country of'. We find that the mechanistic story behind factual recall is more complex than previously thought. It comprises several distinct, independent, and qualitatively different mechanisms that additively combine, constructively interfering on the correct attribute. We term this generic phenomena the additive motif: models compute through summing up multiple independent contributions. Each mechanism's contribution may be insufficient alone, but summing results in constructive interfere on the correct answer. In addition, we extend the method of direct logit attribution to attribute an attention head's output to individual source tokens. We use this technique to unpack what we call `mixed heads' -- which are themselves a pair of two separate additive updates from different source tokens.

papers.title: Attention Heads of Large Language Models: A Survey
papers.core_contribution: This survey paper provides a comprehensive review of research on attention heads in large language models, introducing a novel four-stage framework (Knowledge Recalling, In-Context Identification, Latent Reasoning, Expression Preparation) to categorize attention head functions and summarizing experimental methods for discovering such heads.
papers.conclusion: The survey consolidates research on attention heads in LLMs, providing a framework for understanding their functions and the methods used to discover them, while highlighting the need for further work on complex tasks, unified frameworks, alignment with human cognition, generalizability, multi-collaboration, and theoretical support.
papers.key_findings:
The paper proposes a four-stage framework (Knowledge Recalling, In-Context Identification, Latent Reasoning, Expression Preparation) inspired by human thought to categorize the functions of attention heads in LLMs.
It provides a detailed taxonomy of special attention heads, categorizing them by their roles in the four stages and the LLM architectures where they were discovered.
The survey summarizes experimental methodologies for discovering attention heads into two main categories: Modeling-Free (Modification-Based and Replacement-Based) and Modeling-Required (Training-Required and Training-Free).
It describes how attention heads collaborate across different stages to solve complex tasks, using the Indirect Object Identification (IOI) task as an example.
The paper outlines current limitations in the field, such as a focus on simple tasks and lack of unified frameworks, and proposes future research directions.
papers.limitation:
Current research primarily focuses on simple tasks, leaving complex reasoning tasks underexplored.
There is a lack of unified frameworks to comprehensively describe the mechanisms of attention heads.
Aligning LLM mechanisms with human cognitive processes remains a significant challenge.
future_direction: Extending research to more complex tasks and real-world applications.
Developing unified frameworks to comprehensively describe attention head mechanisms.
Enhancing alignment between LLM mechanisms and human cognitive processes.
papers.abstract: Since the advent of ChatGPT, Large Language Models (LLMs) have excelled in various tasks but remain as black-box systems. Understanding the reasoning bottlenecks of LLMs has become a critical challenge, as these limitations are deeply tied to their internal architecture. Among these, attention heads have emerged as a focal point for investigating the underlying mechanics of LLMs. In this survey, we aim to demystify the internal reasoning processes of LLMs by systematically exploring the roles and mechanisms of attention heads. We first introduce a novel four-stage framework inspired by the human thought process: Knowledge Recalling, In-Context Identification, Latent Reasoning, and Expression Preparation. Using this framework, we comprehensively review existing research to identify and categorize the functions of specific attention heads. Additionally, we analyze the experimental methodologies used to discover these special heads, dividing them into two categories: Modeling-Free and Modeling-Required methods. We further summarize relevant evaluation methods and benchmarks. Finally, we discuss the limitations of current research and propose several potential future directions.

papers.title: Extending a Mathematical Theory of the Emergence of Knowledge from the Experience to Capture Learning Dynamics in Transformers
papers.research_question: How do transformers' learning dynamics emerge from the structure of training data, and how does this relate to human semantic development?
papers.core_contribution: Extends a mathematical theory of learning dynamics to minimal transformers, demonstrating that learning trajectories are predictable from data structure and mirror human semantic development.
papers.conclusion: The work provides initial steps toward understanding how transformers learn, demonstrating that experience guides learning in a way that mirrors human semantic development, and the mathematical theory helps capture these dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
Learning occurs in two phases: fast reduction of loss-between via relation information, and slower reduction of loss-within via item information through attention.
Learning dynamics follow sigmoidal trajectories for dataset dimensions, as predicted by deep linear network theory.
The model exhibits progressive differentiation of concepts, learning broader categories before finer ones.
The model shows U-shaped learning for certain features, such as overgeneralization of properties.
Embeddings from the minimal transformer correlate with those from larger LLMs, suggesting relevance to scaled-up models.
papers.limitation: The study uses a simplified toy dataset and minimal transformer architecture, which may not fully capture complexities of natural language and larger models.
future_direction: Extending models and training sets to more natural language datasets.
Exploring how attentional strategies emerge for handling longer contextual dependencies.
papers.abstract: The Transformer architecture used in LLMs has garnered widespread attention due to these model's human-like conceptual knowledge and language understanding, yet understanding how these models' capabilities result from experience-guided learning, and connecting this learning process with the structure in their training data, can seem intractable. Here we present preliminary steps to characterizing the developmental trajectory of a minimal Transformer trained on a next-token prediction task, using a simple dataset with quantifiable uncertainty and a simple, intuitively characterizable structure that captures some aspects of natural semantic structure learned by LLMs from large datasets. We show how the dynamic learning process of this model is a predictable consequence of the structure of the training data, exhibiting attested features of human semantic development, as captured in a theory of neural network learning dynamics (Saxe et. al. 2019) previously used to capture such dynamics in a network originally introduced by Rumelhart & Todd (1993).

papers.title: Estimating Knowledge in Large Language Models Without Generating a Single Token
papers.research_question: Is it possible to estimate how knowledgeable a model is about a certain entity, only from its internal computation?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces KEEN, a simple probe trained over internal subject representations to estimate an LLM's knowledge about an entity, correlating with QA accuracy and factuality metrics without generating text.
papers.conclusion: KEEN offers a simple and interpretable solution for entity knowledge estimation from internal representations, which is reflective of model behavior and can guide decisions such as when to apply retrieval or further training.
papers.key_findings:
KEEN correlates with QA accuracy (0.58-0.68) and FActScore (0.66-0.77) across multiple models.
KEEN scores decrease as the fraction of per-entity questions that a model hedges on increases.
KEEN faithfully reflects changes in the model's knowledge after fine-tuning.
A vocabulary projection variant of KEEN (VP-50) is interpretable and highlights a small set of tokens indicative of knowledge clusters and gaps.
KEEN QA probes generalize to predict factuality in open-ended generation, showing transfer across settings.
papers.limitation:
KEEN does not identify the presence or lack of knowledge about specific facts, only estimates overall knowledge about a subject.
KEEN focuses on estimating knowledge for entities, and not all subjects of questions are entities.
The evaluation focuses only on transformer-based auto-regressive LLMs.
future_direction: Develop a more fine-grained approach that predicts how knowledgeable the model is about specific aspects of the subject.
Extend KEEN to handle non-entity subjects.
Study the applicability of KEEN to other model architectures (e.g., Mamba).
papers.abstract: To evaluate knowledge in large language models (LLMs), current methods query the model and then evaluate its generated responses. In this work, we ask whether evaluation can be done before the model has generated any text. Concretely, is it possible to estimate how knowledgeable a model is about a certain entity, only from its internal computation? We study this question with two tasks: given a subject entity, the goal is to predict (a) the ability of the model to answer common questions about the entity, and (b) the factuality of open-ended responses generated by the model about the entity. Experiments with a variety of LLMs show that KEEN, a simple probe trained over internal subject representations, succeeds at both tasks - correlating with both the QA accuracy of the model per-subject and FActScore, a recent factuality metric in open-ended generation. Moreover, KEEN naturally aligns with the model's hedging behavior and faithfully reflects changes in the model's knowledge after fine-tuning. Lastly, we show a more interpretable yet equally performant variant of KEEN, which highlights a small set of tokens indicative of clusters and gaps in the model's knowledge. Being simple and lightweight, KEEN can be leveraged to guide decisions such as when it is appropriate to apply further training or augment queries with retrieval.

papers.title: Retentive or Forgetful? Diving into the Knowledge Memorizing Mechanism of Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the memorizing dynamics of language models, and how does pre-training affect their memory ability?
papers.core_contribution: Pre-training transforms language models from forgetful to retentive by enabling long-term memory formation, influenced by knowledge relevance and diversity.
papers.conclusion: Vanilla language models are forgetful, pre-training leads to retentive models, and knowledge relevance and diversification significantly influence memory formation.
papers.key_findings:
Vanilla language models are forgetful with short memory duration and limited capacity.
Pre-trained language models are retentive and can gradually memorize knowledge through repetitive learning.
Pre-training is crucial for developing long-term memory ability in language models.
There is memory competition between highly relevant knowledge types in pre-trained models.
Lack of knowledge diversity causes memory collapse in early learning stages.
future_direction: Investigate the underlying reasons for the forgetful-retentive transition during pre-training.
Explore other critical factors affecting memorization beyond pre-training and diversity.
Compare memorization mechanisms between language models and the human brain.
papers.abstract: Memory is one of the most essential cognitive functions serving as a repository of world knowledge and episodes of activities. In recent years, large-scale pre-trained language models have shown remarkable memorizing ability. On the contrary, vanilla neural networks without pre-training have been long observed suffering from the catastrophic forgetting problem. To investigate such a retentive-forgetful contradiction and understand the memory mechanism of language models, we conduct thorough experiments by controlling the target knowledge types, the learning strategies and the learning schedules. We find that: 1) Vanilla language models are forgetful; 2) Pre-training leads to retentive language models; 3) Knowledge relevance and diversification significantly influence the memory formation. These conclusions are useful for understanding the abilities of pre-trained language models and shed light on designing and evaluating new learning and inference algorithms of language models.

papers.title: Roles and Utilization of Attention Heads in Transformer-based Neural Language Models
papers.research_question: How are basic linguistic properties captured with the attention heads across transformer-based models and used for downstream tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes an analysis method to understand where linguistic properties are learned and represented in attention heads of transformer architectures, and shows that selecting and concatenating influential attention heads can improve performance on downstream tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that understanding the roles of attention heads can lead to adaptive sentence representations that improve downstream task performance, and reveals internal behaviors of transformer models during fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
Different attention heads on different layers are specialized for different linguistic properties (syntactic, semantic, surface).
The last layer of transformer encoders is not always the best for representing linguistic properties; earlier layers often dominate.
Concatenating the outputs of the top-n influential attention heads (selected via probing) yields better sentence representations and improves downstream task performance.
During fine-tuning, the initial superior attention heads remain influential and their performance is amplified, while adjacent heads also show increased performance.
Attention heads handle both syntactic and semantic information in a balanced way, with a linear relationship between their syntactic and semantic scores.
future_direction: Investigation of how heat maps vary during extensive pre-training to understand the dynamics of the learning processes.
papers.abstract: Sentence encoders based on the transformer architecture have shown promising results on various natural language tasks. The main impetus lies in the pre-trained neural language models that capture long-range dependencies among words, owing to multi-head attention that is unique in the architecture. However, little is known for how linguistic properties are processed, represented, and utilized for downstream tasks among hundreds of attention heads inside the pre-trained transformerbased model. For the initial goal of examining the roles of attention heads in handling a set of linguistic features, we conducted a set of experiments with ten probing tasks and three downstream tasks on four pre-trained transformer families (GPT, GPT2, BERT, and ELECTRA). Meaningful insights are shown through the lens of heat map visualization and utilized to propose a relatively simple sentence representation method that takes advantage of most influential attention heads, resulting in additional performance improvements on the downstream tasks.

papers.title: The Vector Grounding Problem
papers.research_question: Can large language models (LLMs) have internal states and outputs that are referentially grounded in the world, i.e., have intrinsic meaning, despite being trained only on text data without direct interaction with the world?
papers.core_contribution: Argues that large language models can achieve referential grounding (intrinsic meaning) through selection processes in training that endow internal states with representational functions, even without multimodality or embodiment.
papers.conclusion: LLMs can, in principle and in some cases in practice, have internal states and outputs that are referentially grounded, thus solving the Vector Grounding Problem and possessing intrinsic meaning independently of human interpretation.
papers.key_findings:
Distinguishes referential grounding from other forms (sensorimotor, relational, communicative, epistemic) and argues referential grounding is the only kind essential to solving the Vector Grounding Problem.
Proposes that referential grounding requires two conditions derived from teleosemantic theories: causal-informational relations to the world and a history of selection that endows internal states with the function of carrying this information.
Argues that post-training (e.g., preference tuning for factual accuracy) can establish selection processes that confer world-involving representational functions to LLM internal states.
Suggests that pre-training might, under specific conditions, also lead to world-involving representational functions through implicit extra-linguistic success conditions in the training data.
Contends that in-context learning could, in principle, allow LLMs to acquire world-involving representational functions during inference without parameter updates.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) produce seemingly meaningful outputs, yet they are trained on text alone without direct interaction with the world. This leads to a modern variant of the classical symbol grounding problem in AI: can LLMs' internal states and outputs be about extra-linguistic reality, independently of the meaning human interpreters project onto them? We argue that they can. We first distinguish referential grounding -- the connection between a representation and its worldly referent -- from other forms of grounding and argue it is the only kind essential to solving the problem. We contend that referential grounding is achieved when a system's internal states satisfy two conditions derived from teleosemantic theories of representation: (1) they stand in appropriate causal-informational relations to the world, and (2) they have a history of selection that has endowed them with the function of carrying this information. We argue that LLMs can meet both conditions, even without multimodality or embodiment.

papers.title: VISIT: Visualizing and Interpreting the Semantic Information Flow of Transformers
papers.research_question: How can we interpret and visualize the semantic information flow inside transformer language models, particularly focusing on attention heads and memory values?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a tool for visualizing the semantic information flow in transformer language models as an interactive flow graph, and provides new insights into layer norms as semantic filters and the existence of regularization neurons.
papers.conclusion: The work introduces a tool to visualize the semantic information flow in transformers using the logit lens, demonstrates its utility by revealing insights about layer norms and regularization neurons, and validates the approach by supporting other analyses.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads' semantics can be projected via the OV circuit, and only the heads with the largest norms dominate the block's output.
Memory values with the highest attention scores capture the semantics of their corresponding attention head.
Layer normalization layers act as semantic filters, demoting function words and promoting content words in the residual stream.
Regularization neurons exist that are consistently highly activated, have high entropy, and may serve as a constant bias or regularization term.
The flow-graph visualization tool can qualitatively replicate mechanistic analyses, such as indirect object identification, and reveal internal information flow patterns.
papers.limitation:
Limited to English language models, particularly GPT models with multi-head attention, and insights might not generalize to other languages or datasets.
Projection methods and the intersection score Ik have limitations in capturing semantic connections between different tokens with the same meaning.
Pruning based on the assumption that the most activated neurons determine the final prediction might be misleading as less activated neurons could also be relevant.
The methods are not causal and do not employ interventions, so further investigation is needed to fully understand the mechanisms.
future_direction: Apply causal interventions to verify the findings.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in interpretability suggest we can project weights and hidden states of transformer-based language models (LMs) to their vocabulary, a transformation that makes them more human interpretable. In this paper, we investigate LM attention heads and memory values, the vectors the models dynamically create and recall while processing a given input. By analyzing the tokens they represent through this projection, we identify patterns in the information flow inside the attention mechanism. Based on our discoveries, we create a tool to visualize a forward pass of Generative Pre-trained Transformers (GPTs) as an interactive flow graph, with nodes representing neurons or hidden states and edges representing the interactions between them. Our visualization simplifies huge amounts of data into easy-to-read plots that can reflect the models' internal processing, uncovering the contribution of each component to the models' final prediction. Our visualization also unveils new insights about the role of layer norms as semantic filters that influence the models' output, and about neurons that are always activated during forward passes and act as regularization vectors.

papers.title: Decoding In-Context Learning: Neuroscience-inspired Analysis of Representations in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do LLM embeddings and attention representations change following in-context learning, and how do these changes mediate improvement in behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a neuroscience-inspired framework using Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) and Attention Ratio Analysis (ARA) to show that in-context learning improves task-critical representations and attention allocation, which correlate with behavioral gains.
papers.conclusion: ICL improves task-critical representations and attention allocation to relevant content in the prompt, and these representational changes are correlated with behavioral gains.
papers.key_findings:
ICL leads to changes in prompt embedding similarity matrices to better encode task-critical information, which in turn improves behavior.
ICL increases the decodability of task-critical information (e.g., line slope) from embeddings via probing classifiers.
ICL shifts attention to relevant content in the prompt (increased attention ratio to informative parts), which correlates with behavioral improvement.
These representational changes are consistent across multiple layers (except the first) in both Llama-2 and Vicuna models.
The proposed methods (RSA and ARA) provide scalable tools for analyzing latent representations in large language models.
future_direction: Study the effects of ICL on improving planning behavior in LLMs by analyzing latent representations before and after ICL in planning tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable performance improvement through in-context learning (ICL) by leveraging task-specific examples in the input. However, the mechanisms behind this improvement remain elusive. In this work, we investigate how LLM embeddings and attention representations change following in-context-learning, and how these changes mediate improvement in behavior. We employ neuroscience-inspired techniques such as representational similarity analysis (RSA) and propose novel methods for parameterized probing and measuring ratio of attention to relevant vs. irrelevant information in Llama-2 70B and Vicuna 13B. We designed two tasks with a priori relationships among their conditions: linear regression and reading comprehension. We formed hypotheses about expected similarities in task representations and measured hypothesis alignment of LLM representations before and after ICL as well as changes in attention. Our analyses revealed a meaningful correlation between improvements in behavior after ICL and changes in both embeddings and attention weights across LLM layers. This empirical framework empowers a nuanced understanding of how latent representations shape LLM behavior, offering valuable tools and insights for future research and practical applications.

papers.title: Jailbreak Antidote: Runtime Safety-Utility Balance via Sparse Representation Adjustment in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we balance safety and utility in large language models against jailbreak attacks by adjusting internal states during inference?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Jailbreak Antidote, a method for real-time safety-utility balance by sparsely adjusting internal states during inference, showing that safety information is sparsely distributed and adjusting approximately 5% of the state is as effective as modifying the entire state.
papers.conclusion: Jailbreak Antidote offers a lightweight, scalable solution for real-time safety adjustments in LLMs by directly manipulating internal states, enhancing safety while preserving utility and opening new possibilities for real-time safety mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Safety-related information in LLMs is sparsely distributed; adjusting approximately 5% of the internal state is as effective as modifying the entire state.
Jailbreak Antidote achieves high defense success rates (DSR) across nine LLMs and ten jailbreak attack methods.
The method preserves model utility, maintaining high Win Rates on AlpacaEval while enhancing safety.
The approach is efficient, introducing negligible computational overhead and no additional token cost during inference.
The safety direction can be identified via PCA on hidden states from benign and harmful prompts.
papers.limitation:
The method requires pre-defined scaling factor α and sparsity parameter k; dynamically adapting these based on context or model confidence could improve flexibility.
Smaller models are inherently limited by their reduced parameter space, which may restrict the extent of safety adjustment.
Developing robust mechanisms to counter adversaries capable of explicitly exploiting the adjustments in internal states remains an open challenge.
future_direction: Dynamically adapting the scaling factor α and sparsity parameter k based on context or model confidence.
Addressing extreme adversarial settings where attackers explicitly exploit the internal state adjustments.
Investigating the applicability of the approach to other aspects of model alignment, such as fairness or domain adaptation.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) become integral to various applications, ensuring both their safety and utility is paramount. Jailbreak attacks, which manipulate LLMs into generating harmful content, pose significant challenges to this balance. Existing defenses, such as prompt engineering and safety fine-tuning, often introduce computational overhead, increase inference latency, and lack runtime flexibility. Moreover, overly restrictive safety measures can degrade model utility by causing refusals of benign queries. In this paper, we introduce Jailbreak Antidote, a method that enables real-time adjustment of LLM safety preferences by manipulating a sparse subset of the model's internal states during inference. By shifting the model's hidden representations along a safety direction with varying strengths, we achieve flexible control over the safety-utility balance without additional token overhead or inference delays. Our analysis reveals that safety-related information in LLMs is sparsely distributed; adjusting approximately 5% of the internal state is as effective as modifying the entire state. Extensive experiments on nine LLMs (ranging from 2 billion to 72 billion parameters), evaluated against ten jailbreak attack methods and compared with six defense strategies, validate the effectiveness and efficiency of our approach. By directly manipulating internal states during reasoning, Jailbreak Antidote offers a lightweight, scalable solution that enhances LLM safety while preserving utility, opening new possibilities for real-time safety mechanisms in widely-deployed AI systems.

papers.title: A Peek Into the Memory of T5: Investigating the Factual Knowledge Memory in a Closed-Book QA Setting and Finding Responsible Parts
papers.research_question: Which parts of the Transformer-based T5 model are responsible for reaching answers in a closed-book question answering setting?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a head importance scoring method (grad_avg) and uses it to show that in T5 models for closed-book QA, the query component of attention is crucial, knowledge is unevenly distributed, and the encoder and decoder have distinct roles.
papers.conclusion: The study provides insights into how Transformer-based T5 operates in closed-book QA, highlighting the importance of attention components and the uneven distribution of factual knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
The query component of attention is the most important for correcting predictions and reaching answers.
The encoder finds the embedding space of the desired answer entity, while the decoder generates the textual representation.
Knowledge is not evenly distributed in the model; some attention heads are more important than others.
Importance maps are similar across different datasets due to shared pre-training knowledge.
Different named entity types have similar importance distributions based on their semantic similarity.
papers.limitation:
Computational costs prevent verifying all hypotheses about model behavior changes.
Results may be dependent on the three experimented datasets.
future_direction: Experiment with other datasets, including ones with different domains.
Investigate other Transformer-based language models.
Study how models work on NLP tasks with context, such as open-book QA.
papers.abstract: Recent research shows that Transformer-based language models (LMs) store considerable factual knowledge from the unstructured text datasets on which they are pre-trained. The existence and amount of such knowledge have been investigated by probing pre-trained Transformers to answer questions without accessing any external context or knowledge (also called closed-book question answering (QA)). However, this factual knowledge is spread over the parameters inexplicably. The parts of the model most responsible for finding an answer only from a question are unclear. This study aims to understand which parts are responsible for the Transformer-based T5 reaching an answer in a closed-book QA setting. Furthermore, we introduce a head importance scoring method and compare it with other methods on three datasets. We investigate important parts by looking inside the attention heads in a novel manner. We also investigate why some heads are more critical than others and suggest a good identification approach. We demonstrate that some model parts are more important than others in retaining knowledge through a series of pruning experiments. We also investigate the roles of encoder and decoder in a closed-book setting.

papers.title: How do Large Language Models Understand Relevance? A Mechanistic Interpretability Perspective
papers.research_question: How do large language models understand and operationalize the concept of relevance? Specifically, (i) whether there exist common components in LLMs that encode relevance signals independent of specific tasks, and (ii) how these relevance signals are conveyed within the LLMs during the forward pass.
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers a multi-stage, progressive process by which LLMs assess relevance: early layers extract query and document information, middle layers process relevance information according to instructions, and later layers utilize specific attention heads to generate relevance judgments.
papers.conclusion: This paper provides insights into the internal mechanisms of relevance assessment in LLMs using mechanistic interpretability, laying groundwork for more interpretable and trustworthy AI technologies for information retrieval.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs process and transmit relevance information in a progressive manner: early layers capture semantic information from documents and queries, middle layers integrate them with task instructions, and later layers control the output format via specific attention heads.
The mechanism for relevance assessment is universal across pointwise and pairwise prompt formats, and consistent across different LLMs (Llama, Mistral, Qwen).
Specific attention heads (e.g., L15H4 and L31H1 in Llama) are critical for controlling the output format (e.g., generating 'yes' or 'no').
Attention heads capture the interaction between query and document tokens, and this interaction is a key component in modeling relevance signals.
Knockout experiments show that ablating a small set of identified attention heads significantly degrades performance in relevance judgment and document ranking tasks, demonstrating their necessity.
papers.limitation:
The analysis focuses on how the model handles the task of relevance judgment at a structural level, rather than at the level of semantics and knowledge, due to the diversity of documents and queries.
Some identified components (e.g., at the query position) have relatively limited effects on downstream tasks, and their specific roles warrant further investigation.
The identified components are necessary but not proven to be sufficient or minimal for completing the relevance judgment task.
The study does not explore how LLMs acquire the capacity for relevance judgment during pre-training or post-training.
future_direction: Further analysis using different techniques at the knowledge level to understand semantic and knowledge aspects of relevance.
Investigating the specific roles of components with diminished effects (e.g., query position).
Identifying a minimal circuit that is sufficient for the relevance judgment task.
Validating whether fine-tuning enhances the same internal mechanisms for relevance assessment.
papers.abstract: Recent studies have shown that large language models (LLMs) can assess relevance and support information retrieval (IR) tasks such as document ranking and relevance judgment generation. However, the internal mechanisms by which off-the-shelf LLMs understand and operationalize relevance remain largely unexplored. In this paper, we systematically investigate how different LLM modules contribute to relevance judgment through the lens of mechanistic interpretability. Using activation patching techniques, we analyze the roles of various model components and identify a multi-stage, progressive process in generating either pointwise or pairwise relevance judgment. Specifically, LLMs first extract query and document information in the early layers, then process relevance information according to instructions in the middle layers, and finally utilize specific attention heads in the later layers to generate relevance judgments in the required format. Our findings provide insights into the mechanisms underlying relevance assessment in LLMs, offering valuable implications for future research on leveraging LLMs for IR tasks.

papers.title: Physics of Language Models: Part 3.1, Knowledge Storage and Extraction
papers.research_question: How do language models memorize knowledge during training, and extract it later to answer questions or perform logical reasoning during inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that knowledge augmentation (e.g., paraphrasing, sentence shuffling) in pretraining data is crucial for reliable knowledge extraction via instruction fine-tuning, and introduces linear probing techniques to explain this phenomenon.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes with practical recommendations for LLM pretraining: data rewriting (augmentation) is important, and including instruction-like data in pretraining is beneficial.
papers.key_findings:
Mixed training (pretraining on both biographies and QA data) enables knowledge extraction, but the model learns in an abnormal way (first from QA then correlates with BIO).
Without knowledge augmentation in pretraining, instruction fine-tuning fails to extract knowledge (0% accuracy).
Knowledge augmentation (e.g., paraphrasing, sentence shuffling, translations) during pretraining enables knowledge extraction after fine-tuning.
Linear probing shows that knowledge augmentation causes knowledge to be linearly encoded in the hidden embeddings of entity names, whereas without augmentation it is distributed across tokens.
Including celebrity data (with augmentation) in pretraining improves knowledge extraction for minority data (without augmentation).
future_direction: Studying logical reasoning and knowledge manipulation
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can store a vast amount of world knowledge, often extractable via question-answering (e.g., "What is Abraham Lincoln's birthday?"). However, do they answer such questions based on exposure to similar questions during training (i.e., cheating), or by genuinely learning to extract knowledge from sources like Wikipedia? In this paper, we investigate this issue using a controlled biography dataset. We find a strong correlation between the model's ability to extract knowledge and various diversity measures of the training data. $\textbf{Essentially}$, for knowledge to be reliably extracted, it must be sufficiently augmented (e.g., through paraphrasing, sentence shuffling, translations) $\textit{during pretraining}$. Without such augmentation, knowledge may be memorized but not extractable, leading to 0% accuracy, regardless of subsequent instruction fine-tuning. To understand why this occurs, we employ (nearly) linear probing to demonstrate a strong connection between the observed correlation and how the model internally encodes knowledge -- whether it is linearly encoded in the hidden embeddings of entity names or distributed across other token embeddings in the training text. This paper provides $\textbf{several key recommendations for LLM pretraining in the industry}$: (1) rewrite the pretraining data -- using small, auxiliary models -- to provide knowledge augmentation, and (2) incorporate more instruction-finetuning data into the pretraining stage before it becomes too late.

papers.title: What Makes Language Models Good-enough?
papers.research_question: What architectural features, specifically the number of layers and self-attention heads, make language models learn human-like good-enough language processing?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that language models with shallower depth and fewer attention heads can exhibit human-like good-enough language processing, indicating that deep architectures are not necessary for such performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that shallow transformer architectures can achieve human-like good-enough language processing, while the role of attention heads remains unclear.
papers.key_findings:
Models with shallower depth and fewer attention heads can learn good-enough language processing, similar to full models.
Increasing the number of layers from 8 to 12 does not significantly improve human-like good-enough performance.
The number of attention heads does not clearly contribute to models' good-enough performance, contradicting the hypothesis about working memory.
Human accuracy decreases with increased memory load, and models show a similar pattern, especially for items with correct no answers.
The GELP dataset effectively captures good-enough language processing phenomena in humans and models.
papers.limitation:
Model coverage is limited to BERT.
Use of templates in dataset creation may result in unnatural sentences.
Does not test whether models can perform in a human-like way in terms of both grammatical knowledge and good-enough language processing.
future_direction: Generalizing findings to other Transformer-based models such as GPT-2.
Testing whether models can learn the human-like balance between robust and heuristic language processing.
papers.abstract: Psycholinguistic research suggests that humans may build a representation of linguistic input that is 'good-enough' for the task at hand. This study examines what architectural features make language models learn human-like good-enough language processing. We focus on the number of layers and self-attention heads in Transformers. We create a good-enough language processing (GELP) evaluation dataset (7,680 examples), which is designed to test the effects of two plausibility types, eight construction types, and three degrees of memory cost on language processing. To annotate GELP, we first conduct a crowdsourcing experiment whose design follows prior psycholinguistic studies. Our model evaluation against the annotated GELP then reveals that the full model as well as models with fewer layers and/or self-attention heads exhibit a good-enough performance. This result suggests that models with shallower depth and fewer heads can learn good-enough language processing.

papers.title: The Hidden Uncertainty in a Neural Networks Activations
papers.research_question: Does the distribution of a neural network's latent representations correlate with epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty, and can it be used to estimate uncertainty without modifying the training procedure?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework for estimating both epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty from the latent representations of neural networks without modifying the training procedure, showing that deeper layers yield uncertainty estimates similar to established methods like MC Dropout and Deep Ensembles.
papers.conclusion: The hidden activations of neural networks contain information about both aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty. Uncertainty proxies derived from density estimates of deep layers closely follow those of established methods, enabling wide application and rapid deployment without retraining.
papers.key_findings:
Epistemic uncertainty can be identified with the negative log-likelihood (surprise) of observing a particular latent representation.
Aleatoric uncertainty can be quantified via the entropy of the predictive distribution derived from output-conditional latent densities.
Deeper layers yield epistemic uncertainty estimates that behave similarly to established but computationally expensive methods (e.g., MC Dropout, Deep Ensembles).
Shallow layers yield more conservative epistemic uncertainty estimates, which are better for out-of-distribution detection but worse for calibration near the training data distribution.
Additional regularization (e.g., a reconstruction loss) improves out-of-distribution detection performance but leads to ambiguous calibration close to the training data distribution.
papers.limitation:
Feature collapse can make activations of out-of-distribution data indistinguishable from training data.
High-dimensional densities are challenging to estimate.
Additional regularization improves out-of-distribution detection but leads to ambiguous calibration near the training data distribution.
future_direction: Aggregating uncertainty information from several layers for out-of-distribution detection.
papers.abstract: The distribution of a neural network's latent representations has been successfully used to detect out-of-distribution (OOD) data. This work investigates whether this distribution moreover correlates with a model's epistemic uncertainty, thus indicates its ability to generalise to novel inputs. We first empirically verify that epistemic uncertainty can be identified with the surprise, thus the negative log-likelihood, of observing a particular latent representation. Moreover, we demonstrate that the output-conditional distribution of hidden representations also allows quantifying aleatoric uncertainty via the entropy of the predictive distribution. We analyse epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty inferred from the representations of different layers and conclude that deeper layers lead to uncertainty with similar behaviour as established - but computationally more expensive - methods (e.g. deep ensembles). While our approach does not require modifying the training process, we follow prior work and experiment with an additional regularising loss that increases the information in the latent representations. We find that this leads to improved OOD detection of epistemic uncertainty at the cost of ambiguous calibration close to the data distribution. We verify our findings on both classification and regression models.

papers.title: Towards Fully Exploiting LLM Internal States to Enhance Knowledge Boundary Perception
papers.research_question: Can LLMs estimate their confidence using internal states before response generation to save computational resources, and how can we improve their perception of knowledge boundaries?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs can estimate confidence before generation, saving computation, and the introduced C3 method improves their ability to recognize unknown questions, enhancing reliability.
papers.conclusion: LLMs can predict the correctness of their answers prior to generation, providing a cost-efficient approach, and C3 substantially improves their ability to recognize what they do not know and consistently enhances their overall perception.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs can perceive their knowledge boundaries before generating a response, and post-generation states further enhance perception.
The gap between pre- and post-generation perception remains stable across question difficulties, task formats, amount of generated content, and training set sizes.
C3 significantly improves LLMs' perception of what they do not know, increasing the unknown perception rate.
papers.limitation:
The research is based on binary confidence; more fine-grained confidence is needed.
The work focuses on factual knowledge boundaries; non-factual knowledge boundaries require further investigation.
Experiments are only on 7B and 13B models; effectiveness on larger models remains to be validated.
future_direction: Exploration of more fine-grained confidence.
Investigation of the model's perception of its non-factual knowledge boundaries.
Validation of the approach on larger models.

papers.title: The Mechanics of Conceptual Interpretation in GPT Models: Interpretative Insights
papers.research_question: What are the observable representation patterns that characterise conceptual interpretation within language models? Can we localise specialised representational patterns to derive an interpretation model within language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces concept editing, a variation of knowledge editing, to uncover conceptualization mechanisms in LLMs, and through analysis of MLP, MHA, and hidden states, reveals distinct patterns of semantic processing.
papers.conclusion: The work elucidates how transformer models process semantic information through distinct component interactions, paving the way for targeted interventions and improved interpretability techniques.
papers.key_findings:
MLP layers employ key-value retrieval and context-dependent processing, focusing on specific lexical and semantic features.
MHA layers show distributed nature with higher-level activations, suggesting sophisticated semantic integration.
Hidden states emphasize the importance of the last token and top layers in the inference process, indicating gradual information building.
Concept interpretation involves a collaborative process among model components, with compositionality being critical.
Patterns are consistent across languages (English and Spanish) and across alternative definitions, indicating robust processing strategies.
papers.abstract: Locating and editing knowledge in large language models (LLMs) is crucial for enhancing their accuracy, safety, and inference rationale. We introduce ``concept editing'', an innovative variation of knowledge editing that uncovers conceptualisation mechanisms within these models. Using the reverse dictionary task, inference tracing, and input abstraction, we analyse the Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP), Multi-Head Attention (MHA), and hidden state components of transformer models. Our results reveal distinct patterns: MLP layers employ key-value retrieval mechanism and context-dependent processing, which are highly associated with relative input tokens. MHA layers demonstrate a distributed nature with significant higher-level activations, suggesting sophisticated semantic integration. Hidden states emphasise the importance of the last token and top layers in the inference process. We observe evidence of gradual information building and distributed representation. These observations elucidate how transformer models process semantic information, paving the way for targeted interventions and improved interpretability techniques. Our work highlights the complex, layered nature of semantic processing in LLMs and the challenges of isolating and modifying specific concepts within these models.

papers.title: Truth-value judgment in language models: 'truth directions' are context sensitive
papers.research_question: How does context affect the truth-value probes in large language models, and are these probes coherently incorporating contextual information?
papers.core_contribution: Truth-value probes are context sensitive but also sensitive to irrelevant information, and truth-value directions causally mediate natural language inference.
papers.conclusion: Truth-value directions are context sensitive and causally mediate inference, but probes are not fully coherent.
papers.key_findings:
Truth-value probes are sensitive to context, but also to irrelevant information.
The type of errors (consistency errors) depend on the layer, model, and data.
Probes trained without premises (no-prem) still show context sensitivity, indicating that prior beliefs are not represented independently.
Instruction-tuned models show different error patterns (more E4 errors) compared to pretrained-only models.
Truth-value directions causally mediate natural language inference (intervention experiment).
papers.abstract: Recent work has demonstrated that the latent spaces of large language models (LLMs) contain directions predictive of the truth of sentences. Multiple methods recover such directions and build probes that are described as uncovering a model's "knowledge" or "beliefs". We investigate this phenomenon, looking closely at the impact of context on the probes. Our experiments establish where in the LLM the probe's predictions are (most) sensitive to the presence of related sentences, and how to best characterize this kind of sensitivity. We do so by measuring different types of consistency errors that occur after probing an LLM whose inputs consist of hypotheses preceded by (negated) supporting and contradicting sentences. We also perform a causal intervention experiment, investigating whether moving the representation of a premise along these truth-value directions influences the position of an entailed or contradicted sentence along that same direction. We find that the probes we test are generally context sensitive, but that contexts which should not affect the truth often still impact the probe outputs. Our experiments show that the type of errors depend on the layer, the model, and the kind of data. Finally, our results suggest that truth-value directions are causal mediators in the inference process that incorporates in-context information.

papers.title: From Loops to Oops: Fallback Behaviors of Language Models Under Uncertainty
papers.research_question: What is the connection between undesirable LLM behaviors (hallucinations, degenerate text, repetitions) as fallbacks under epistemic uncertainty, and how do they shift with model strength and during generation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that fallback behaviors (sequence repetitions, degenerate text, hallucinations) follow a consistent ordering and shift from simpler to more complex forms as model strength increases (via more parameters, pretraining tokens, or instruction tuning), and during a single generation as uncertainty rises.
papers.conclusion: Fallback behaviors are inherent to LLMs under epistemic uncertainty, and current decoding methods that reduce degenerate text often increase subtler and potentially more harmful hallucinations, making model uncertainty harder to detect.
papers.key_findings:
Larger models (more parameters) shift fallback behavior from sequence repetitions to hallucinations.
Models that train longer (see more pretraining tokens) shift from repetitions to hallucinations.
Instruction finetuning shifts fallback behaviors from repetitions to hallucinations.
During a single generation, models shift from correct answers to hallucinations and then to repetitions as uncertainty increases.
Random sampling (e.g., temperature sampling) reduces repetitions but increases hallucinations.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often exhibit undesirable behaviors, such as hallucinations and sequence repetitions. We propose to view these behaviors as fallbacks that models exhibit under epistemic uncertainty, and investigate the connection between them. We categorize fallback behaviors - sequence repetitions, degenerate text, and hallucinations - and extensively analyze them in models from the same family that differ by the amount of pretraining tokens, parameter count, or the inclusion of instruction-following training. Our experiments reveal a clear and consistent ordering of fallback behaviors, across all these axes: the more advanced an LLM is (i.e., trained on more tokens, has more parameters, or instruction-tuned), its fallback behavior shifts from sequence repetitions, to degenerate text, and then to hallucinations. Moreover, the same ordering is observed during the generation of a single sequence, even for the best-performing models; as uncertainty increases, models shift from generating hallucinations to producing degenerate text and finally sequence repetitions. Lastly, we demonstrate that while common decoding techniques, such as random sampling, alleviate unwanted behaviors like sequence repetitions, they increase harder-to-detect hallucinations.

papers.title: Diversity of Transformer Layers: One Aspect of Parameter Scaling Laws
papers.research_question: How do the internal layer dynamics (specifically the diversity of layer outputs) in Transformers relate to parameter scaling laws?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that diversity of predictions from each module in the Transformer residual stream is crucial for performance, and that adding layers improves performance only when layers are diverse, with diminishing returns that align with parameter scaling laws.
papers.conclusion: The diversity of predictions from each module on the residual stream is important for improving Transformer performance, and the effectiveness of adding layers diminishes as the number of layers increases, consistent with parameter scaling laws.
papers.key_findings:
Performance improves when individual layers make predictions close to the correct answer and remain mutually diverse.
